submission.name: Money Rehearsal
submission.tagline: Practice a tough money conversation out loud before you have it for real.
submission.inspiration: Asking a bank or financial aid office about fees, missed payments, or a confusing notice can be intimidating. We wanted to make a low-pressure place to practice asking those questions and saying what you need. The project is a rehearsal tool, not financial advice.
submission.what_it_does: Users can speak through a short practice conversation with an AI office representative, then hear a spoken reply. The prompts focus on everyday banking and student account situations, such as asking for a fee explanation. We also tried camera based expression cues, but they can misread faces and should not be treated as reliable feedback.
submission.how_we_built_it: A React interface sends speech through ElevenLabs transcription to a Flask service, which passes the text and conversation context to Gemini for a response. ElevenLabs then speaks the answer back so the practice feels conversational. Our camera experiment uses OpenCV for rough expression signals, but it is an optional input and not needed for the main flow.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Camera expression estimates are inconsistent, especially with lighting and different faces, and audio transcription sometimes gets names or amounts wrong. The conversation loop works, but the expression feature can make it less dependable.
submission.accomplishments: We connected speech input, generated replies, and spoken responses in a working practice loop. We also built a basic screen for choosing a banking scenario.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how audio transcription and speech playback fit into a web conversation, and saw why facial expression guesses need careful limits.
submission.whats_next: We would test the scenarios with financial educators and make the voice and camera options easier to adjust or turn off. We also want clearer boundaries so the tool directs users to a real bank representative for account specific decisions.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides central voice interaction for practice conversations, but transcription and expression features add complexity and unreliability.

submission.name: Trail Pantry
submission.tagline: Pack a better day trip with the food and supplies you already have.
submission.inspiration: Before a day hike or campus outing, it is easy to forget what snacks and supplies are already packed. We adapted a pantry helper idea for people planning short outdoor trips, where a quick inventory can make packing less stressful.
submission.what_it_does: Trail Pantry lets users photograph items, save them to a trip kit, and ask Gemini for simple snack or packing suggestions based on the list. It has a mobile-friendly inventory and a chat screen, though image scans sometimes miss items or label them incorrectly.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Expo and React Native with TypeScript for the app, Firebase for sign-in and saved kits, and a FastAPI backend in Python. Google Cloud Vision identifies likely objects from a photo, then Gemini uses the saved list to suggest combinations and practical packing ideas. The app sends requests through the backend so keys stay off the client.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The scan results can be inconsistent, especially with cluttered photos, and the app occasionally shows a stale kit after saving. We also had to work through differences between browser and mobile behavior.
submission.accomplishments: We connected photo scanning, saved trip kits, and Gemini suggestions in a usable mobile flow. The main screens are in place, and a user can build and revisit a basic packing list.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a helpful AI suggestion depends on getting reliable inventory data first. We also got more practice tracing state and authentication issues across a mobile app and backend.
submission.whats_next: We would improve scan editing, add expiry and quantity fields, and make suggestions account for dietary needs and trip length.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini provides meaningful packing suggestions based on user inventory, but image recognition inconsistencies limit core functionality.

submission.name: Trail Jam
submission.tagline: Race your friends to set up camp before the weather turns.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to turn the scramble of getting ready for an outdoor trip into a small, chaotic game. Instead of campus parking, the setting is a crowded campground where players try to claim a spot and get their gear in place.
submission.what_it_does: Trail Jam is a short Unity game where players steer around obstacles, compete for campsite spaces, and gather scattered gear before time runs out. It runs from start to finish, though collisions and item pickups can behave inconsistently when several objects overlap.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Unity and C# for movement, collisions, and the timed round, with Photoshop for the simple art assets. GitHub helped us share the project and merge scene changes. Audio and background movement add a little atmosphere to the playable loop.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Unity scene changes were awkward to merge, and balancing movement with collisions took repeated adjustments. We still have cases where a pickup does not register on the first pass.
submission.accomplishments: We built a complete playable round with a clear goal and a playful campground setting. We are happy with how the menu and game screen fit together.
submission.what_we_learned: We got more comfortable building gameplay in Unity and coordinating shared project files. We also learned that small physics bugs can make a short game feel much harder to finish.
submission.whats_next: We would add more campground layouts, pause and audio controls, and a few gear-based power-ups.

challenge_results.rationale: The game has a clear goal and playful setting but lacks detailed technical explanations and has inconsistent mechanics.

submission.name: Form Compass
submission.tagline: Turn campus paperwork into a short checklist and listenable plain language guide.
submission.inspiration: As students, we keep running into forms for housing, financial aid, and campus services that are hard to parse when deadlines are close. We wanted to make those documents feel less intimidating and help someone spot what they need to do next.
submission.what_it_does: Upload a document to see its original text next to a simpler explanation and a checklist of possible next steps. Gemini also labels the kind of document and creates a short walkthrough that can be played aloud. We focused the demo on student facing forms rather than every kind of technical document.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made a React and Vite web interface with a Node and Express backend. The backend sends extracted document text to Gemini for a plain language rewrite and action list, then stores the result in MongoDB Atlas for the page to retrieve. ElevenLabs turns the explanation into audio. The upload, explanation, and playback pieces work, though the flow between them still needs cleanup.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Connecting the upload, AI response, database, and audio service took more time than expected. We also had to keep the rewrite readable without letting it lose important details, and our current demo does not handle every document layout reliably.
submission.accomplishments: We got the main document explanation flow running and made a page that can show the source alongside the simpler version. We are proud that Gemini is doing the central rewrite and checklist work, with audio available as another way to consume the result.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that clear prompts and predictable response structure matter when the UI depends on AI output. Gemini helped us draft and refine the summaries, but we still needed to check the results and design around gaps in document extraction.
submission.whats_next: We would improve support for scanned and longer documents, add a way to choose a reading level, and let students save useful explanations. We would also spend more time testing whether the checklist makes the next steps easier to find.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini central to document simplification and checklist generation with audio output, but extraction and flow issues limit core completeness.

submission.name: TrailTalk
submission.tagline: A pocket audio guide that narrates the places you pass on a walk.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make local walks more interesting for people who do not want to keep checking a map or reading plaques. A spoken guide seemed like a good fit for visitors exploring a campus or neighborhood at their own pace.
submission.what_it_does: TrailTalk is a mobile friendly guide that plays short spoken descriptions for stops along a walking route. Pick a route and a narration style, then the app uses nearby stop information to generate commentary and reads it with an ElevenLabs voice. The route and audio are connected through a lightweight web view, so you can keep listening while you walk.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built the interface in React and used the browser location and map view to show a small set of stops. An Express backend receives the selected stop and its notes, then calls Gemini through OpenRouter to write a concise narration. The backend passes that text to ElevenLabs and returns the audio for playback, which keeps the API keys away from the phone UI. Our Python helper handles transcript and stop data prep for the demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the narration and audio ready quickly enough for a walk was tricky because the services respond at different speeds. Location updates can also jump around, so the app sometimes selects a nearby stop unexpectedly. Our current routes have a small hand-entered set of places, and the experience can fail if an API call times out.
submission.accomplishments: We connected stop selection, generated narration, and voice playback into a working demo. We are happy with how ElevenLabs makes short descriptions feel like an actual guide instead of another block of text.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much audio timing affects a mobile experience: even a good voice feels awkward if it arrives too late. Gemini helped us vary the narration, while we learned to give it compact stop notes so it would stay focused and brief.
submission.whats_next: We would cache audio for common stops, improve location handling, and let local groups add their own route notes. We would also test more narration styles and add a clear way to pause or replay a stop while walking.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides central voice narration for walking tours but has timing and location accuracy issues.

submission.name: Garden Gauge
submission.tagline: A small GPS tracker that helps campus gardeners see how far their watering route takes them.
submission.inspiration: We wanted a simple way for volunteers tending several campus garden beds to track their walking routes and compare weekly effort. Bike tracking gave us a starting point, but we adapted the display for a garden cart and short rounds between plots.
submission.what_it_does: The device records a route's distance and current speed from GPS and sends the totals to a small web leaderboard for the week's garden rounds. A map view shows the recorded route so volunteers can see which beds they visited.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used an ESP32 with a GPS reader to collect location points and calculate distance and speed between updates. The board sends the totals to a web service that stores weekly volunteer entries and orders them by distance. Google Maps displays the route from the saved location data.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The GPS receiver could take a while to get a usable fix, especially near buildings. We made the enclosure from a quick 3D print and had to adjust it so the wiring and battery would fit.
submission.accomplishments: We got the tracker sending route totals to the site and displaying the route on a map. We are proud that the hardware and leaderboard work together for a full garden round.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how noisy GPS readings can be over short distances and how much the enclosure design matters once the electronics need to fit inside it.
submission.whats_next: We would add a more reliable GPS antenna and a button to mark a garden stop. A clearer volunteer view for comparing different routes would also be useful.

submission.name: SignSafe
submission.tagline: Practice everyday money decisions with spoken prompts and a simple fraud alert coach.
submission.inspiration: We wanted a low pressure way for people to practice spotting suspicious payment situations without needing to read a long lesson. We also wanted the practice to work as an audio interaction for users who prefer listening or have difficulty using text heavy screens.
submission.what_it_does: SignSafe presents short transaction scenarios and asks the user to decide whether something seems unusual. It uses a lightweight outlier check on scenario details to flag suspicious patterns, then an AI coach explains the warning in plain language and reads it aloud. Users can practice with voice or tap through the choices.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a React mobile web interface and a FastAPI backend in Python. The backend checks transaction fields against simple anomaly rules and sends the scenario and result to a language model for a short explanation. ElevenLabs generates the spoken coach response, and the frontend plays it after each answer so the user can review the reasoning. The transaction examples are demo data, not a connection to real bank accounts.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: It was hard to make the fraud flags understandable without implying that a simple rule can confirm fraud. The voice call also adds delay, and the demo can get stuck waiting for audio if the service is slow. We kept the examples small and the risk explanation basic so the flow would work end to end.
submission.accomplishments: We connected practice scenarios, anomaly flags, explanations, and spoken feedback in one mobile friendly demo. We are proud that the audio is part of the main learning loop rather than an afterthought.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to distinguish a suspicious signal from a definitive fraud finding and to explain that difference in the interface. Building around ElevenLabs also taught us to keep spoken responses short enough to fit the pace of a practice session.
submission.whats_next: We would add more scenario types, improve the rules with safer example data, and let users adjust the pace of the audio coach. A future version could include a clearer history of which warning signs the learner has practiced.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is central to the learning loop with spoken feedback, but the audio integration has delays and limited scenario variety.

submission.name: Focus Beacon
submission.tagline: A desk companion that notices when your focus drifts and offers a small market news break.
submission.inspiration: We liked the idea of a physical reminder that can bring someone back from a distracting screen without blocking their work. We paired that with a brief stream of financial headlines so a break could be guided by a topic the user chose.
submission.what_it_does: A small desk display uses webcam attention cues to change its expression when someone appears to look away for a while. A separate dashboard can show a handful of recent market headlines and use Gemini to turn one into a short spoken summary. The pieces are demonstrated separately today, so headlines do not yet affect the physical companion.
submission.how_we_built_it: The hardware prototype uses Raspberry Pi Pico W boards, a small LCD, a motor, and a cardboard housing. A local React and TypeScript page captures webcam frames and sends them to a Python service using MediaPipe face landmarks to estimate whether the user is looking away; the service updates the companion state through MongoDB. We also built a web dashboard that loads sample market headlines and asks Gemini for a brief summary. The news view is currently a separate demo path, and its audio playback is not connected to the desk device.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The Pico Wi-Fi setup and screen libraries took time to get working, and we switched from acrylic to cardboard when fabrication became impractical. MediaPipe gave us more useful face landmarks than our first approach, but looking away is only a rough signal for distraction. The headline dashboard and the hardware state still need an integration pass.
submission.accomplishments: We made the physical display respond to the webcam based attention estimate and built a separate Gemini headline summary page. We are proud of the homemade enclosure and the working path from camera frames to a visible companion state.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to keep a fallback fabrication plan and to test hardware libraries early. Gemini was useful for turning a headline into a short explanation, while we learned that adding a cloud feature does not automatically make it part of the device experience.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the headline summaries to the desk display, add spoken playback, and make the attention cue easier to adjust. We would also test the hardware on a more stable network and improve the enclosure.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini provides a meaningful secondary function by summarizing headlines, but the core attention tracking and physical display operate separately.

submission.name: Study Sentinel
submission.tagline: A tiny desk companion that nudges library study groups back to their work.
submission.inspiration: We built this for students who settle into long study sessions and lose track of how often they drift away from their screens. Browser blockers felt too easy to ignore, so we wanted a small physical presence that could offer a visual reminder without interrupting the whole table.
submission.what_it_does: A webcam checks whether a student appears to be looking away, then updates a small desk device with a pixel expression and a gentle visual cue. The team also made a simple web page to show the current focus state; it does not yet handle multiple people reliably.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and TypeScript page to capture webcam frames and send them to a Python service, where MediaPipe estimates eye direction. A MongoDB store keeps the latest status, and two Pico W boards, an LCD, a motor, and a cardboard enclosure make up the desk companion. We also tried Databricks with a small set of session events to summarize when focus changes happened, but that analysis is still a separate demo from the device loop.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the Pico boards online was unreliable on campus Wi-Fi, so we used a hotspot during the demo. The webcam check can mistake a glance away for distraction, and the Databricks summary is not yet connected back to the live interface.
submission.accomplishments: We got the browser, Python service, database, and physical display working together for a basic single-user session. We are proud that the cardboard build and the pixel expressions made the idea tangible, even with the rough edges.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much time hardware setup and network access can take away from web integration. MediaPipe gave us more useful eye landmarks than our first OpenCV attempt, and Databricks helped us explore session patterns, though we have more work to do before it can guide the product.
submission.whats_next: We would make the focus signal configurable, improve handling for different lighting and camera angles, and connect the session summaries to the web page. A sturdier enclosure and a clearer privacy flow would also help before using it in shared study spaces.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used for session event analysis but not yet connected to the main product flow, giving it a minor role.

submission.name: Branch Buddy
submission.tagline: A quick guide to the next step in your everyday banking task.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to help people who are unsure which banking option or service fits a situation, especially when they are trying to sort something out quickly. The project takes the idea of matching a purchase to a card and applies it to common financial questions and branch services.
submission.what_it_does: Users can pick a situation, such as replacing a card or asking about a transfer, and see a suggested service path with a short spoken explanation. The prototype uses a small set of mocked banking options, and the voice playback is demonstrated separately from the service flow.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made a web interface with React and Next.js, a Node backend, and a small JSON catalog of banking tasks and options. Plaid Sandbox data was used to explore account context, while an ElevenLabs voice demo reads sample guidance; login, account context, and audio are not fully connected.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Connecting sandbox account data to a reliable login flow took longer than expected, and the prototype still relies on mock task mappings. The spoken guidance does not yet update dynamically from a user's account details.
submission.accomplishments: We built the core screens for choosing a banking situation and comparing suggested paths, plus a separate voice sample that makes the guidance easier to follow. We also established a basic data shape for the service catalog.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that financial recommendations need clear context and careful wording, and that adding voice creates another integration step beyond generating audio. AI tools helped us sketch and refine sample explanations, but the service recommendations remain rule-based.
submission.whats_next: We would connect account context, login, recommendations, and ElevenLabs playback into one flow, then expand and review the service catalog with clearer explanations and safeguards.

challenge_results.rationale: Branch Buddy improves a financial process by guiding users through banking tasks with voice explanations, but its mock data and disconnected components limit full functionality.

submission.name: RepReady
submission.tagline: A voice-first workout partner for students learning the basics of strength training.
submission.inspiration: We kept hearing classmates ask whether they were doing a lift correctly, especially when the campus gym was busy and no trainer was nearby. We wanted to make beginner guidance easier to access without turning every workout into a complicated plan. The idea became a small coaching tool that can talk someone through a routine and help them keep track of how it felt. We focused on students fitting exercise around classes, limited equipment, and uneven experience.
submission.what_it_does: RepReady lets a user enter a fitness goal and available equipment, then suggests a short routine with practical technique reminders. Gemini helps turn those constraints into a simple session and adjusts suggestions based on a user's feedback afterward. ElevenLabs reads the plan and reminders aloud so users can listen between sets instead of staring at a screen. The app also records completed sessions and basic notes. It is not reliable enough to judge live lifting form, so its guidance stays general.
submission.how_we_built_it: We kept the seed's Python and Google ADK agent structure, with separate steps for planning, coaching language, and follow-up suggestions. Gemini handles the prompt-based routine and adapts it to the user's stated goals and equipment. We send the resulting reminders to ElevenLabs for spoken playback, while Railway and Docker provide the app's deployment setup. A small Databricks notebook groups session notes by exercise and shows which reminders come up most often, giving us a basic data view to inform prompt changes. These pieces work together in the demo, though the notebook data flow is still fragile.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: It was difficult to keep advice concise while still making each exercise understandable. Gemini sometimes returned inconsistent exercise names, which made the spoken reminders awkward or mismatched to the routine. The voice playback also occasionally lagged behind the plan screen. Our analytics depend on a small set of manually entered session records, so the Databricks view is not a strong basis for broad conclusions. We could not validate whether the suggestions are appropriate for every user's health or ability.
submission.accomplishments: We got a basic flow working from a student's equipment and goal to a suggested routine and spoken reminders. We are proud that audio is part of the coaching experience rather than an unrelated add-on. We also connected a simple view of exercise notes to the planning work, which gave us a way to inspect the kinds of advice the app produces. The prototype is small, but it gives us a useful starting point for campus fitness support.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that an AI coach needs a narrow job and careful wording to avoid sounding more certain than it should. Connecting generated plans to audio exposed naming and timing issues that were easy to miss in text-only testing. We used AI coding tools to sketch agent steps and debug integration problems, then had to simplify their suggestions when they added too much complexity. We also saw how messy even a small collection of workout notes can be when trying to summarize it.
submission.whats_next: We would like to add clearer onboarding for ability and equipment, plus a way to save routines between visits. We also want to make audio playback controls more dependable and let users ask for a reminder again without replaying the full plan. More structured session data could support a more useful Databricks analysis. Any future form feedback would need careful validation before it could be treated as safety guidance.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is central to the voice-first coaching experience, but technical challenges remain in audio timing and consistency.

submission.name: ShiftLedger
submission.tagline: Keep track of shift clothes, care notes, and the outfit you need for a workday.
submission.inspiration: For students balancing campus jobs and classes, getting ready for a shift can mean checking the weather, remembering a uniform detail, and figuring out when work clothes need washing. We borrowed the idea of a visual closet but aimed it at people who rotate a small set of work outfits. We wanted a quick way to organize those items and make mornings a little less guessy. We also saw a chance to make outfit planning useful for students preparing for interviews or service shifts.
submission.what_it_does: ShiftLedger lets users add clothing photos and label items for a job, interview, or campus event. A weather panel can show current conditions, while a separate outfit suggestion panel offers combinations from the saved items. Gemini is used for a small part of photo labeling, but those results do not reliably flow into the outfit suggestions yet. ElevenLabs can read a saved care note or reminder aloud. We also mocked a monthly clothing-spend summary to connect wardrobe planning with budgeting, though it is not linked to a bank account.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React Native and Expo for the mobile screens, with on-device storage for saved clothing entries and image handling. The weather lookup feeds its own card, and Gemini photo labels appear in a separate inventory view. ElevenLabs reads care notes through a simple playback action. A basic budget summary screen is currently populated with sample entries rather than connected transactions. These components demonstrate the intended pieces, but they are not yet joined into one dependable recommendation flow.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The main issue was coordinating features that each worked on their own but shared different data shapes. Photo labels did not consistently match the categories expected by the outfit screen. Image sizing and mobile storage took time, and the weather panel could fail without a clear message. The BNY-related budget screen is only a mock, so it cannot provide real spending insights. Gemini's role is limited in this version, and its labels still need review.
submission.accomplishments: We built several working mobile screens for a closet inventory, local weather, and spoken care reminders. We are glad the project has a clear use case for students who need to prepare for work as well as class. We also made a first pass at connecting wardrobe choices with clothing costs. The demo shows the pieces we want to bring together, even though the full flow is unfinished.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that separate features can look complete while still failing to share useful data. Mobile image handling also took more care than we expected. AI tools helped us draft the labeling prompt and get a basic voice playback working, but they did not solve the integration details. We need simpler shared data structures before adding more screens.
submission.whats_next: Next we would connect the inventory labels to outfit suggestions and make the app handle missing or uncertain labels clearly. We would replace the sample budget entries with an intentional manual spending tracker, without requiring bank access. We also want to add a reliable way to edit care notes and replay them. A later version could test whether the pieces save time during a real workweek.

submission.name: Aid Atlas
submission.tagline: Map nearby student support services and keep track of practical campus resources.
submission.inspiration: Students often need to find a place that can help with food, transit, or short-term financial support, but the information is spread across different pages. We wanted to make nearby options easier to browse on a map and let campus groups add useful listings. The idea applies an event-style map to resource discovery, where location and opening details matter. We kept the scope to a small searchable directory for the weekend.
submission.what_it_does: Aid Atlas displays campus-area support resources as map pins and lets users submit a listing with its location and basic details. Users can search by name or category and open a card with address information. We included a small financial-services section for resources such as budgeting help and emergency aid offices. The app works from submission through browsing, but location lookup can return imprecise results and listings are not verified. There is no account system yet.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and TypeScript frontend with Leaflet for the map and a Node/Express backend backed by MongoDB and Mongoose. The form sends a resource name, category, description, and coordinates to the backend, which stores records and serves them to the search view. OpenCage helps turn an entered address into a map location, and the user can adjust the pin before submitting. Keeping the financial-help listings in the same record format makes them searchable alongside other campus resources. We spent time on the interface in Figma and used Tailwind for styling.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Address geocoding was inconsistent, especially when a user entered a building name without a full address. The search results can also include listings outside the intended campus area. We had trouble with MongoDB Atlas configuration and did not finish deployment, so the demo depends on a local setup. Users can submit inaccurate information because we have not built verification or moderation. The map sometimes takes a moment to reflect a newly added pin.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a working resource form, backend storage, search, and map display. We are proud of the pin-adjustment flow because it lets a submitter correct a rough address result. The financial support category also gives the project a focused use beyond a generic map directory. We learned enough about Leaflet and MongoDB to build a useful end-to-end prototype.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how map libraries, geocoding services, and database records fit together in a web app. MongoDB queries and search behavior took more iteration than we expected. We also saw that a resource directory needs a plan for keeping information current and trustworthy. Figma helped us settle the main screens before we connected the backend.
submission.whats_next: We would add login and a review process for new listings, then verify addresses and opening hours. Better search filters could help students narrow results by service type and distance. We also want to deploy the app so campus groups can try adding resources. A later version could include links to official financial aid and budgeting information.

challenge_results.rationale: Aid Atlas improves campus resource discovery with a map-based directory including financial support listings, but lacks verification and has geocoding issues.

submission.name: PairPort
submission.tagline: Share a live view of your lab setup so a teammate can point, click, and help troubleshoot.
submission.inspiration: We wanted classmates in data and computing labs to be able to get help without crowding around one screen. A shared view with remote input seemed useful for walking through a bug or showing a confusing workflow.
submission.what_it_does: PairPort captures a host's screen and lets a connected viewer send mouse and keyboard input while the host keeps working. We also tried a simple session label so teams could tell which lab task they were looking at, but the full demo did not connect end to end.
submission.how_we_built_it: The prototype uses Python with MSS for screen capture, OpenCV and Pillow for image handling, PySide6 for the desktop interface, and PyAutoGUI for input events. We used Pyngrok while exploring connections and AI coding tools for planning and code suggestions; the capture and input pieces run separately, but we did not get a reliable complete streaming session.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting screen frames and remote input to stay responsive at the same time was harder than expected, and the pieces did not come together into a working demo. Generated code also added extra complexity, so we spent time trimming it and narrowing the feature set.
submission.accomplishments: We got isolated screen-capture and input experiments running and learned what a shared troubleshooting tool needs. We are proud we explored a practical use for remote interaction even though the integrated flow remained unfinished.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned the basics of MSS, PyAutoGUI, and handling image frames, along with how much network timing affects an interactive session. ChatGPT helped us shape the scope, while Claude and Copilot offered code suggestions that still needed careful review.
submission.whats_next: We would first connect capture, viewing, and input in one stable local-network session, then measure and reduce delay. After that, we would consider audio and remote connections beyond the same Wi-Fi network.

submission.name: ClearCue
submission.tagline: A spoken second opinion for suspicious links and pages, with risk patterns organized for review.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to help people who find technical scam warnings hard to interpret, especially when a message or webpage feels urgent. A short spoken explanation could give someone a moment to pause before sharing information.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype scans page text and domain clues for possible impersonation or pressure tactics, then presents a plain-language warning and an optional ElevenLabs narration. We also explored using Databricks to organize flagged signals for analysis, but scanning, analytics, and the voice flow are separate pieces rather than one complete extension experience.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used TypeScript, HTML, and CSS for a browser-extension interface, with Google Safe Browsing as a reputation signal and Groq for explanation experiments. ElevenLabs can narrate a warning, while a Databricks notebook was used to explore how extracted risk indicators might be grouped; that notebook does not yet feed results back into the extension.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: A few broad text rules flagged harmless pages, and reputation checks did not catch every suspicious example. We also ran out of time to connect the notebook output to the extension and to make narration state behave consistently, so the demo only shows parts of the intended flow.
submission.accomplishments: We built separate pieces for webpage signals, readable warning text, and spoken output. We are glad the project keeps its focus on helping a person understand why something may be risky instead of showing only a score.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that simple keywords do not provide enough context for reliable scam detection, and that explanation quality affects whether a warning is useful. Gemini-style language analysis and ElevenLabs voice both need to fit a controlled flow; we used AI coding and generation tools as aids, but had to review outputs and keep the components small.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the analytics work to the browser scan results and test the extension on more varied examples. We also want to improve domain context, reduce false alarms, and make the voice controls more predictable.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides optional voice narration for scam warnings, a meaningful secondary feature that requires user activation but is not central to the core functionality.

submission.name: LabEntry
submission.tagline: A prototype check-in screen that helps campus workshop teams remember required protective gear.
submission.inspiration: In student workshops, people may step into a task quickly and forget a basic piece of protective equipment. We wanted to see whether a simple entry check could make reminders easier for lab staff and students.
submission.what_it_does: A user can enter a PIN or scan an RFID badge, and a camera experiment looks for selected safety gear before showing a status on a web dashboard. We also tried ElevenLabs narration for a missing-item reminder; the badge, vision, dashboard, and audio components work as separate demonstrations, and we did not connect them into a complete checkpoint.
submission.how_we_built_it: The web dashboard uses React and TypeScript, with Node.js, Express, Socket.io, and MongoDB experiments for user and event data. A Flask service uses Python and OpenCV with a YOLO-based PPE detector, and we explored Gemini for explaining a result and ElevenLabs for spoken reminders. The intended flow was badge or PIN input to a camera check, then a dashboard update and optional voice prompt, but the integrations were still incomplete.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The camera model was inconsistent under our setup, and Wi-Fi and laptop compatibility made it difficult to keep the vision and web pieces aligned. We also had merge conflicts and did not finish the live update path between the checkpoint and dashboard.
submission.accomplishments: We got several useful components started, including a badge and keypad input experiment, a PPE recognition model experiment, and a dashboard layout. The spoken reminder idea gave us a concrete way to make a basic status feel more understandable.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how many details are involved in connecting Python vision code with a Node web service and a database. We also got introductory experience with serial input and Socket.io, and saw that AI explanations and generated voice need a dependable detection result before they can help.
submission.whats_next: We would first connect the badge flow, camera result, and dashboard event so one check can be followed from start to finish. Then we would improve detection under varied lighting and make the voice reminder optional and concise.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is used as an optional add-on for a spoken reminder outside the main user flow, with components working separately but not connected into a complete checkpoint.

submission.name: MoneyWords
submission.tagline: Practice the language of everyday banking with short, personalized lessons and spoken examples.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make common financial language less intimidating for people who are learning English while settling into new communities. Banking forms and account conversations can be difficult to follow when the vocabulary is unfamiliar, so we built around small, practical learning moments.
submission.what_it_does: The planned site uses a short onboarding quiz to estimate a learner's English level and track unfamiliar terms, then offers financial vocabulary cards, short scenarios, and a guided practice conversation. Gemini can help draft examples and ElevenLabs can read them aloud, but the learning tools and personalized vocabulary state are not yet joined into one working flow.
submission.how_we_built_it: The web prototype combines an Astro and React interface styled with Tailwind and Shadcn with a Go backend and Firebase experiments. The intended path is for the frontend to send a learner's level and terms to the backend, which stores progress and requests Gemini-generated banking examples; ElevenLabs audio is a separate playback experiment. We also tried Docker, AWS, and Vercel in the deployment setup, but did not complete an integrated service.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Several of these tools were new to us, especially Go, and onboarding plus saved vocabulary took longer to plan than expected. We also hit Gemini API limits while experimenting and did not finish wiring the voice and content features to learner progress.
submission.accomplishments: We shaped a focused language-learning idea around everyday financial tasks and made early interface and backend pieces. We are proud that we explored how vocabulary practice could connect to practical banking situations without claiming the prototype is ready for real financial guidance.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a useful learning flow needs consistent progress data as well as generated content, and that the frontend and backend contracts have to be settled early. Gemini helped us explore examples, while ElevenLabs gave us a way to test spoken vocabulary; both still need validation and integration.
submission.whats_next: We would connect onboarding, saved terms, scenario practice, and audio into a single lesson path. We would also review examples for clarity and accuracy with people familiar with the financial tasks before expanding the content.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini is used to draft examples but not yet integrated with the learning flow, giving relevance 3 as a meaningful step.

submission.name: GearTurn
submission.tagline: Turn the equipment you already own into a simple plan for your next outdoor repair.
submission.inspiration: We noticed that small outdoor projects often stall because people cannot remember what supplies they have or which task to start with. We wanted to adapt a pantry-style inventory and guided-step flow for student clubs maintaining bikes and camping gear.
submission.what_it_does: GearTurn is meant to track repair supplies, their condition, and when they may need attention, then suggest a small repair based on available materials and the time someone has. A guided mode breaks a repair into steps with timers, and voice entry is intended to make logging gear faster. The inventory, recommendations, and voice experiments remain loosely connected, so the full repair flow is not working end to end.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React and TypeScript for the interface, Node.js for a backend experiment, and MongoDB for inventory data. The planned flow starts with a user adding parts manually or by voice through ElevenLabs, then sends the saved inventory and constraints to a recommendation step that uses Gemini to select a repair guide. The backend is intended to return structured steps to the frontend, where a guided session can display instructions and timers; currently those parts are mocked or run separately.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The main difficulty was turning vague entries such as a partly used tube of sealant into consistent inventory data that recommendations could use. Voice recognition and parsing need a confirmation step, and we did not finish connecting the saved inventory, suggestion logic, and repair session into one reliable path. We also had to keep the project small enough to describe real maintenance without pretending the suggestions are expert instructions.
submission.accomplishments: We made a first pass at an inventory and repair-planning interface and explored how voice input could reduce the effort of recording supplies. We are proud of the problem framing for club equipment, where using what is already on hand can make a small fix more approachable.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that recommendation quality depends on a clean model for parts, condition, and task constraints, not only on adding AI. Structured outputs and a quick review step matter when voice input is uncertain. We also learned to make component boundaries clear: the interface collects data, the backend should preserve it, and the recommendation stage needs to explain which supplies it expects to use.
submission.whats_next: We would connect inventory entry through repair guidance and add a way to confirm or correct parsed voice entries. Later, we would ask experienced club members to review the repair steps and broaden the catalog to common bike and camping gear maintenance.

challenge_results.rationale: The project adapts a pantry-style inventory for outdoor gear repairs with voice entry and AI recommendations, but the full flow is not end-to-end working.

submission.name: Parcel Quest
submission.tagline: Explore underused city blocks and weigh the tradeoffs of turning them into homes.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make city planning feel more tangible by letting people explore what could happen to overlooked lots. We were interested in infill housing, but wanted to show that a promising parcel also has costs, constraints, and neighborhood effects.
submission.what_it_does: Parcel Quest lets a user choose an area and browse possible infill sites on a map. Gemini helps summarize each candidate’s apparent suitability across site conditions, development feasibility, housing potential, and environmental impact, then the app ranks the options and shows the reasoning and source notes. A small overview panel compares a few sustainability measures so users can inspect the tradeoffs.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Python with FastAPI for the API and React, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the map interface. The backend sends candidate parcel information to Gemini for structured summaries and scores, then returns ranked results and notes for the frontend to display. We also added a basic validation view to make it easier to see which inputs informed a result.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting suggested places to line up with the correct locations on the map took repeated coordinate fixes. Some parts of the demo work in isolation, but the full flow from area search through ranked results does not consistently complete. Parcel details and environmental estimates also need stronger source checks before anyone could use them for real planning.
submission.accomplishments: We put together a working map view and a first pass at comparing candidate sites across several factors. We are proud that the project exposes its reasoning instead of presenting a single unexplained score.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much parcel scoring depends on uncertain data and assumptions about zoning, costs, and neighborhood needs. Gemini helped us organize messy candidate information into a consistent format, but we still had to check the outputs and design the ranking logic ourselves.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the search and ranking pieces into a reliable end-to-end flow and cache previous area results. We would also improve parcel boundaries and add clearer links to authoritative zoning and environmental data.

submission.name: Clinic Case Desk
submission.tagline: Turn scattered clinic intake notes into a reviewable queue with spoken next steps.
submission.inspiration: Student and community clinics often have to sort through intake notes, appointment messages, and follow-up paperwork while keeping staff focused on patients. We wanted to adapt a case dashboard for a setting where a quick spoken summary can help a busy coordinator decide what needs attention.
submission.what_it_does: Clinic Case Desk organizes sample patient cases into a dashboard and uses specialized AI tasks to suggest follow-ups, missing information, or a draft patient message. Staff can accept or dismiss suggestions with a swipe-style control, and ElevenLabs reads a short case summary or selected next step aloud. Suggestions remain review items for staff rather than actions sent automatically.
submission.how_we_built_it: The frontend uses React and Next.js, with a FastAPI service coordinating the case workflow and MongoDB storing case records and review decisions. Gemini-powered agents produce different kinds of case suggestions, while ElevenLabs converts selected summaries into audio for the dashboard. The pieces connect through API calls so a case can be opened, analyzed, reviewed, and played back in one flow.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Connecting MongoDB records to the FastAPI workflow and routing each case to the right agent took the most iteration. We also had to keep the audio focused on short, useful summaries instead of reading every detail. The demo flow works end-to-end with sample cases, but it does not yet handle secure real clinic records or a full intake upload process.
submission.accomplishments: We are proud to have the case queue, agent suggestions, swipe review, and spoken summaries working together in the demo. The voice feature gives coordinators another way to scan a case while they are moving between tasks.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to connect a database-backed dashboard to several focused AI tasks without hiding the review step. Prompting tools helped us draft and revise agent instructions, and building the ElevenLabs playback path taught us to treat audio as part of the workflow rather than an add-on.
submission.whats_next: We would add secure authentication and a controlled way to import intake documents. We would also refine the agent roles and let staff configure which updates are read aloud.

submission.name: Campus Watchtower
submission.tagline: Use a camera view and Gemini to flag possible campus facility incidents for review.
submission.inspiration: A maintenance or safety issue can be easy to miss when it is only reported after someone walks away. We wanted to see whether a small camera-based prototype could help campus operations staff notice possible incidents sooner.
submission.what_it_does: Campus Watchtower analyzes a selected camera image or short feed sample with Gemini and labels possible issues such as smoke, blocked access, or an unusual crowd. It shows the location on a map and offers a suggested route to inspect the area. The output is a review prompt for staff, not an automatic emergency dispatch.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Next.js for the dashboard and API, MongoDB for incident records, and Gemini for image and text analysis. A separate Python process checks the configured camera sample and posts candidate events, which the dashboard maps and turns into an inspection suggestion.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Working with low-quality or changing camera views made incident labels inconsistent, so results still need human review. The prototype runs through the demo flow, though it has only been exercised with a small set of configured feeds and does not cover a broad live camera network.
submission.accomplishments: We connected image analysis, an incident list, and mapped inspection routes into one usable prototype. We also made the uncertainty visible by presenting detections as candidates to verify.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that image quality and camera placement shape what a model can reasonably identify. Building around hardware feeds also made us think about timing, retries, and how to keep a camera failure from looking like an all-clear.
submission.whats_next: We would test against more varied camera conditions and add better feed health reporting. We would also make route suggestions account for access restrictions and staff availability.

submission.name: Workshop Dash
submission.tagline: Race to spot a lab hazard, with a physical controller that brings the game into your hands.
submission.inspiration: We like quick competitive games and wanted to make a workshop safety scenario feel more interactive than a quiz. A handheld controller seemed like a fun way to connect simple physical movement to decisions on screen.
submission.what_it_does: Two players compete to identify and respond to hazards in a fictional campus workshop. A thick card-shaped controller sends movement and button input to a Godot game, while Gemini provides brief flavor text and alternate descriptions for a round. A small Databricks notebook summarizes the round event log to show which hazard prompts came up most often.
submission.how_we_built_it: The game is built in Godot, with a Raspberry Pi and microcontroller sending serial input through a Python bridge over UDP. Godot uses that input to move each player and trigger actions, while a small Gemini call supplies optional round text. We exported round events to a Databricks notebook for a basic count summary; that analysis is separate from the live controls.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Serial data conversion and controller drivers were difficult to keep stable, and the UDP connection occasionally drops inputs. The game does run end-to-end, but one controller can disconnect after repeated rounds and the animations still look rough. The Databricks piece is only a small post-round summary, not part of the gameplay loop.
submission.accomplishments: We are proud that physical controller actions can affect a playable head-to-head game. We also got a basic event export and summary working alongside the prototype.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much coordination it takes to move input across hardware, Python, and Godot without losing timing. Gemini was useful for short bits of generated flavor, while the Databricks exercise helped us see how simple event logs can become a game balancing clue.
submission.whats_next: We would make controller reconnection more reliable and improve the game feedback for missed inputs. We would also use the round summaries to tune hazard pacing and add more workshop scenarios.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini provides optional flavor text in a game with physical controllers and Godot, showing meaningful secondary use but not central to the core gameplay loop.

submission.name: ScamScore Studio
submission.tagline: Practice spotting suspicious money messages, then turn the warning signs into a short backing track.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to help students learn to question urgent financial messages without making the experience feel like another lecture. We borrowed the idea of generating music around a user’s choices and paired it with a phishing-style message review so the lesson could feel more memorable.
submission.what_it_does: Users review sample bank and payment messages, mark suspicious details, and get a Gemini explanation of signals such as pressure tactics or odd payment requests. The app turns the review into a short musical practice loop with a selectable mood and tempo, and can read the key warning signs aloud with ElevenLabs. A small Databricks workflow groups anonymized practice choices into common warning categories for the demo dashboard.
submission.how_we_built_it: The React and Next.js interface sends a selected message and the user’s marked clues to a Gemini-backed analysis flow, which returns an explanation and structured warning labels. A music generator assembles a simple Strudel loop from those labels and chosen settings, while ElevenLabs speaks a compact recap for accessibility. We store practice events and use a Databricks notebook to summarize category counts, so the dashboard can show what learners are noticing without feeding those counts back as verified threat intelligence.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The full flow works, but music generation sometimes returns code that Strudel cannot play, and the message analysis can overreact to ordinary urgency. We had to keep the examples synthetic and make clear that a score is for practice, not proof that a real message is safe or fraudulent. Getting the audio, analysis, and event summary to agree on the same warning labels took extra glue work.
submission.accomplishments: We connected message review, explainable warning labels, generated music, spoken feedback, and a basic analysis dashboard in one demo. We are proud that a user’s own choices shape the recap instead of receiving only a generic scam warning.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to turn a free-form model answer into structured labels before using it in other components. Gemini helped interpret the wording of sample messages, while our own checks kept the explanation tied to visible clues; ElevenLabs made the recap easier to listen to, and Databricks gave us a way to inspect practice patterns. We also learned that generated music needs strict constraints and a reliable fallback if the code does not compile.
submission.whats_next: We would improve validation for the generated loops and add more message examples across different financial situations. We would also test the warning explanations with people who are new to scam terminology and refine the category dashboard before using anything beyond synthetic practice data.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides a meaningful secondary audio role by reading warning signs aloud for accessibility, but the core experience works without it.

submission.name: CrewSignal
submission.tagline: Match campus event crews to short-term jobs and see which skills open the next door.
submission.inspiration: Campus venues and local event organizers often need several stagehands, lighting techs, or setup crews on short notice. We wanted to make it easier for students with practical skills to find those gigs without sorting through unrelated job listings.
submission.what_it_does: Organizers paste in a shift description and get its key skills and requirements pulled into a structured listing. Students can be ranked against the opening, see missing credentials, and review a suggested next step; organizers can select a group and send interview requests.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and TypeScript frontend with a FastAPI backend and SQLAlchemy models. A centralized Python AI service turns free-form shift posts into validated schemas, and the app stores listings and candidate profiles in PostgreSQL.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting inconsistent event descriptions into predictable fields took careful prompt and schema work, and our suggested training paths are only a first pass. We also had to make tradeoffs around how matching should be priced and how to compete with existing staffing services.
submission.accomplishments: We got the main path working from a pasted job description through structured requirements, ranked candidates, and interview invitations. We are proud that the same flow can point a student toward a missing qualification instead of simply rejecting their application.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that matching depends on representing both a shift’s requirements and a worker’s experience in a useful way. AI-assisted extraction helped us move faster, but we still needed validation and clear rules around the data it produced.
submission.whats_next: We would like to verify licenses and safety credentials, then try the workflow with a few local venues. Longer term, we could add other hands-on roles such as venue maintenance and technical production.

challenge_results.rationale: The project addresses a specific campus need with a structured job matching flow, but similar solutions exist.

submission.name: Pantry Route
submission.tagline: A map of neighborhood food support and shared growing spaces for community volunteers.
submission.inspiration: Volunteer groups coordinating food drives often have to search across separate directories to find pantries, community gardens, and places that accept donations. We wanted a single map that helps organizers plan outreach around the resources already in a neighborhood.
submission.what_it_does: Users choose what kind of food support or community space they are looking for, then browse relevant places on an interactive map. Listings combine public map and food assistance data with community-added markers, and Gemini can create a short plain-language summary of a selected location.
submission.how_we_built_it: The app uses React, Vite, Tailwind, and Leaflet in the browser, with a Python FastAPI service and SQLite for user-created markers. We pull place information from OpenStreetMap and USDA sources, with a Little Free Library feed as another local resource source, and call Gemini for concise listing descriptions.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The source datasets use different categories and can be incomplete, so aligning a listing with the map filters took work. We also hit merge conflicts and Python package setup problems; Gemini summaries help explain a listing, but they do not verify that its details are current.
submission.accomplishments: We brought several public data sources and community markers into one responsive map that volunteers can explore. The key flow from choosing a need to viewing nearby options is connected end to end.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that useful mapping work involves cleaning and reconciling data as much as drawing the map. Gemini gave us a quick way to summarize service descriptions, while API integration and time management shaped much of the weekend.
submission.whats_next: We would like pantry and garden organizers to update their details directly and work with local groups to check listing accuracy. We also want a way to see whether a map search led someone to a useful resource.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini provides a meaningful secondary function by generating summaries, but is not central to the core mapping functionality.

submission.name: Relief Relay
submission.tagline: Ask about a crisis by voice, then turn the answer into a practical aid route.
submission.inspiration: People trying to help during a crisis can have trouble turning scattered reports into a concrete next step. We wanted a voice interface that could explain needs in plain language and help a volunteer think through where supplies might go.
submission.what_it_does: A volunteer asks a spoken question about a selected crisis or region and receives a spoken response with a short summary of reported needs and suggested logistics. A map view highlights aid mismatch by location, and the assistant can outline a more focused response route from the information shown.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made a Flutter client that streams speech through ElevenLabs transcription and speech generation, with a Python Flask service coordinating the conversation and map data. Gemini helps summarize regional information and shape the response, while a map layer displays need and aid indicators; the services run in Docker on Google Cloud.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Keeping spoken responses quick while the model and data lookups run was difficult, and crisis information can be incomplete or out of date. We connected the voice, map, and summary flow, but its recommendations need human review and are not a dispatch system.
submission.accomplishments: We built a working loop from a spoken question to a spoken, location-aware aid summary. The map and voice response give volunteers a shared starting point for discussing where help may be most useful.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how latency accumulates across speech recognition, model calls, and speech playback, and how important it is to keep each step understandable. AI tools helped us prototype the summaries, but joining them to location data and a usable audio flow took most of our integration effort.
submission.whats_next: We would like to connect more reliable, timestamped crisis feeds and make it easier for local aid groups to review suggested routes. With consent, a future version could keep a shareable record of the conversation for coordinating volunteers.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides central voice interaction for crisis aid routing, but latency and data reliability issues remain.

submission.name: Signal Skirmish
submission.tagline: A two-player campus radio race controlled with a chunky, button-filled handheld.
submission.inspiration: We liked the feel of fast card duels and wanted to make a small competitive game where players physically trigger their moves. We shifted the showdown to a campus radio booth, where players race to keep a signal clear while disrupting the other station.
submission.what_it_does: Two players use a homemade controller to send actions into a Godot game, where they try to hold signal quality and outlast their opponent. Gemini adds brief commentary based on the current match, and Databricks was used to inspect sample match events during development.
submission.how_we_built_it: The game runs in Godot, with a Raspberry Pi Pico controller sending serial input to a Python bridge that forwards events over UDP. We used GitHub for version control, Gemini for optional match commentary, and a small Databricks notebook to explore recorded play events.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Serial-to-game input and hardware drivers were finicky, and the controller occasionally misses an action, so the match can feel uneven. We also ran into Godot animation and dependency trouble plus merge conflicts while working in parallel.
submission.accomplishments: We got a physical controller driving a playable two-person game, with hardware inputs reflected in the match. We are happy with the core idea of making a simple duel feel more hands-on.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how input travels from a microcontroller through a Python bridge into a game engine, and how small timing issues can affect play. We also got a basic look at using match data for commentary and analysis.
submission.whats_next: We would like to make controller input more reliable, improve the animations, and tune the opponent behavior. We also want to make the data view useful enough to compare different match strategies.

submission.name: Desk Splashdown
submission.tagline: A voice-powered study timer that spots phone breaks and gives your desk a playful warning.
submission.inspiration: We found it easy to reach for a phone during a long study block, especially when working through difficult classes. We wanted a physical reminder that reacts right away and makes the break feel noticeable without turning the whole session into another app.
submission.what_it_does: A webcam checks for phone use with YOLOv8, then Gemini confirms likely distractions and writes a short nudge aloud through ElevenLabs. An Arduino can trigger a small desk fan as a playful cue, and the program keeps camera processing, AI requests, and hardware control running separately.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Python and OpenCV with YOLOv8 for camera detection, Gemini for the follow-up message, and ElevenLabs text-to-speech for the spoken prompt. An Arduino controls the fan through a relay, while a laptop runs the detection and API calls.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The Raspberry Pi boards we planned to use would not boot reliably, so we moved processing to a laptop and kept the Arduino for the physical response. Detection can still mistake a phone for another object, and the fan response is more of a nudge than a precise distraction measure.
submission.accomplishments: We connected the webcam, AI message, spoken feedback, and hardware cue into a working study-session loop. Splitting the work across threads helped the camera keep updating while the other parts were busy.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned the basics of Arduino control, computer vision, and threading, and saw how hardware and AI calls need to coordinate without blocking each other. ElevenLabs made the feedback audible without requiring us to record a set of prompts ourselves.
submission.whats_next: We would like to make phone detection more dependable and add a way to pause the system when a student needs their phone for classwork. We could also test other gentle physical reminders for different study spaces.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides central voice feedback for study nudges, but detection reliability issues affect core functionality.

submission.name: Goalhouse
submission.tagline: Small daily challenges, shared stakes, steady progress.
submission.inspiration: We kept making plans to improve our routines and then losing momentum after a few days. We wanted a lightweight place to turn personal goals into manageable daily actions and let friends help keep each other accountable.
submission.what_it_does: Goalhouse suggests small tasks across areas like movement, creativity, and social connection based on a short onboarding quiz. Users can check tasks off and write daily reflections; a friend group can also pledge a small stake to a shared goal and see whether members have kept up.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made a React Native app with an Express and Supabase backend for accounts, tasks, and progress. A Cohere-powered coach can respond to questions about a user's goals, while the group pledge idea borrows the accountability mechanic of friends having a stake in one another's follow-through.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We did not get the full demo working end to end: quiz answers, task suggestions, and saved progress were isolated pieces and did not reliably stay in sync. Expo connectivity on public Wi-Fi and merging work across the team also slowed us down, so the friend pledge flow remained a sketch.
submission.accomplishments: We built separate screens for exploring tasks, tracking progress, and reflecting on the day. We are proud that the core interaction is concrete enough to show how a routine app could make consistency feel social.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that personalization needs a clear path from onboarding answers to useful tasks, and that database updates need to be planned alongside the UI. AI assistance helped us iterate on coach responses, but it did not solve integration or state-management issues for us.
submission.whats_next: We would connect quiz results, task generation, and progress storage into a reliable flow before expanding the social feature. Voice reflections and user-created task categories are ideas for a later version.

challenge_results.rationale: The project shows a clear concept of turning personal goals into social accountability but lacks end-to-end functionality and detailed technical explanations.

submission.name: QuietCue
submission.tagline: Turn a few hand signs into clear classroom requests.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to help students communicate simple needs during class when speaking up is uncomfortable or not practical. We focused on a small set of visual cues and spoken output rather than trying to translate every conversation.
submission.what_it_does: A browser prototype uses a webcam to recognize a limited set of hand shapes and phrases, then displays the interpreted text and can read it aloud with ElevenLabs. A separate Gemini chat companion can respond to typed messages with supportive suggestions, though the two parts are not joined in the demo.
submission.how_we_built_it: MediaPipe runs hand landmark detection in the browser, and JavaScript heuristics compare joint positions to recognize selected signs. We connected a Gemini chat view and an ElevenLabs speech call as separate components.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Hand movement sometimes gets mistaken for a held sign, and recognition varies with camera angle and lighting. The chat, hand recognition, and speech output work in isolation, but the complete interaction is not reliably connected.
submission.accomplishments: We got browser-based hand landmarks working and built a small sign-to-text flow with spoken output. We also made a separate chat prototype to explore how a companion could respond to typed requests.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that simple landmark rules need careful handling of movement and hand position. AI tools helped us draft and refine the companion responses, while MediaPipe gave us hands-on experience with local vision processing.
submission.whats_next: We’d expand the sign set with testing from sign language users and connect recognition, text, speech, and chat into one accessible flow. We’d also add controls for choosing which phrases the app recognizes.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides meaningful audio output for recognized signs but is not central to the core interaction.

submission.name: Campus Cushion
submission.tagline: Turn everyday spending into a small buffer for student costs.
submission.inspiration: Small expenses can make it hard for students to set money aside, even when they want to prepare for upcoming costs. We adapted round-up saving into a tool aimed at building a modest buffer for predictable campus expenses.
submission.what_it_does: Campus Cushion reads sample transaction data, rounds purchases up to the next dollar, and totals the difference as savings for a chosen expense such as books or transit. Gemini summarizes spending patterns and suggests a possible adjustment, while the dashboard shows the savings amount and a simulated wallet transfer.
submission.how_we_built_it: A FastAPI service processes transaction records and calculates round-ups, while a React interface presents totals and Gemini-generated explanations. We used the Solana SDK to demonstrate a devnet transfer flow and Nessie sample banking data for transactions.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We had to keep the money calculations consistent across transaction processing and the wallet display, especially for very small amounts. The demo flow works end to end with sample data, but the savings suggestions can be too broad when the transaction history is sparse.
submission.accomplishments: We connected sample banking data, round-up calculations, a Gemini explanation, and a simulated wallet transfer in one working flow. We’re proud that the dashboard shows both the amount set aside and the spending pattern behind it.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that AI summaries are more useful when grounded in a clear transaction breakdown, and that monetary values need precise handling through every step. We also gained experience connecting a financial data flow to a blockchain demo.
submission.whats_next: We’d add goal tracking for recurring campus costs and more useful monthly projections. We’d also improve the suggestions for short or incomplete transaction histories.

challenge_results.rationale: Improves student financial buffers through round-up savings integrated with spending analysis and blockchain demo, though finance is a core feature but not a specific industry process.

submission.name: Pantry Ledger
submission.tagline: Use what’s on hand to plan meals and keep shared kitchen costs visible.
submission.inspiration: Shared apartments often have ingredients in the kitchen but no clear plan for using them, while grocery costs are split informally. We wanted to connect meal planning with a simple view of what a shared household may need to buy.
submission.what_it_does: Users enter available ingredients and get recipe suggestions ranked by how well they match, including missing items and instructions. Gemini can suggest substitutions from the pantry list, and a small shared-cost view estimates what missing ingredients may add to the next grocery trip.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a Next.js and TypeScript frontend with Tailwind styling, and a Python Flask service that matches ingredients against TheMealDB results. Gemini handles substitution suggestions, while the cost panel uses rough item estimates in the app.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Ingredient names and quantities from recipe data are inconsistent, so match scores and cost estimates can be off. The end-to-end flow works, but Gemini sometimes suggests a substitute that doesn’t fit the recipe, and we haven’t made the estimates dependable enough for actual budgeting.
submission.accomplishments: We connected ingredient entry, ranked recipe results, and pantry-based substitution suggestions in a working web app. We also added a basic way to see how missing items might affect a shared grocery plan.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that messy ingredient data affects both recipe matching and any cost estimate built on top of it. Gemini helped us generate substitution ideas, but those suggestions still need checks against the recipe context.
submission.whats_next: We’d improve ingredient normalization, let roommates save a shared pantry, and make grocery cost estimates more consistent. We’d also add a review step for substitutions before they become part of a meal plan.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini's substitution suggestions are central to the meal planning flow, but inconsistent data affects reliability.

submission.name: TraceQuest
submission.tagline: Follow the bug, then coordinate your next move.
submission.inspiration: When code fails a test, it can be difficult to tell which state change caused the problem. We wanted a browser tool that makes execution visible and adds a lightweight team-coordination idea: separate helpers can inspect different clues before forming a debugging plan.
submission.what_it_does: Students can run Python problems in the browser, inspect variable changes and control flow, and get Gemini hints grounded in the error and failing test. A small set of specialist panels summarizes runtime, test, and code clues before a coordinator view suggests a next debugging step.
submission.how_we_built_it: The app uses Next.js with Monaco Editor, and Pyodide runs Python in a browser worker. We convert execution output into structured data for visualizations and Gemini prompts; the specialist panels are simple role-based summaries rather than autonomous agents.
