submission.name: Checkout Compass
submission.tagline: A quick card guide for community organizations buying supplies.
submission.inspiration: Small campus organizations often buy food, equipment, or event supplies without much time to compare which card earns the best rewards. We adapted a card recommendation idea for student treasurers who need a useful answer at checkout, while keeping the tool focused on their organization's approved wallet.
submission.what_it_does: A browser extension prototype looks for checkout signals and suggests a card based on a merchant category and a small set of reward rules. The dashboard lets a treasurer enter cards and review a basic rewards summary; it does not connect to bank accounts or handle payments.
submission.how_we_built_it: The prototype uses a Manifest V3 JavaScript extension, an Express API, and a small card and merchant dataset. We planned Databricks processing for comparing category rewards, Gemini to help interpret ambiguous merchant descriptions, and ElevenLabs to read a recommendation aloud, but these pieces were not connected into one reliable flow.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Checkout pages vary a lot, and our detection only behaves predictably on a few test pages. The recommendation logic, extension panel, and AI services run as separate pieces, so some results are mocked and a suggestion can be missing or miscategorized.
submission.accomplishments: We put together a working slice of checkout detection and a basic card comparison view for organization purchases. We also mapped out how structured rewards data could support a more useful financial workflow for student groups.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that merchant categorization and incomplete card terms can matter more than adding another model call. Gemini helped us explore merchant descriptions, while Databricks and ElevenLabs showed us possible extensions, but connecting services takes more time than making each piece run alone.
submission.whats_next: We would validate the reward data, connect the extension to one stable recommendation API, and add organization-specific spending limits. A more dependable merchant mapping and a complete audio recommendation flow would come after that.

challenge_results.rationale: Checkout Compass addresses a specific financial process for student organizations by suggesting reward-optimized cards during purchases, but its functionality is limited to a basic prototype with disconnected components and mocked results.

submission.name: SpriteStage
submission.tagline: Build a tiny playable world from your own art direction.
submission.inspiration: We wanted a quick way for student artists to turn an idea into a small game without learning a full engine first. Our prototype keeps the editable 2D sandbox and AI sprite creation, but adds a Databricks-backed view of level play data to help creators spot where players get stuck.
submission.what_it_does: Creators can request a sprite, place it with obstacles in a side-scrolling level, and play the result in the browser. A small analytics panel groups recorded play attempts by level section; it is intended to point out trouble spots, though the data view can be slow to refresh.
submission.how_we_built_it: The frontend uses React, Phaser, and Tailwind, with an Express server routing requests to Python scripts for Gemini image generation. We also send sample play events into a Databricks notebook for aggregation and display the resulting section summaries in the editor.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Generated images and level configurations do not always arrive in the same shape, and large sprites sometimes need manual resizing. The analytics refresh can fail when the sample event batch is empty, so the playable editor works more reliably than the insight panel.
submission.accomplishments: We connected the main loop from generating a sprite to placing it in a level and trying the level in the browser. The data summary gives creators a basic way to inspect play attempts without leaving the editor.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much care it takes to pass image assets and game configuration between frontend and backend. Databricks made simple play data easier to summarize, but useful analytics depend on collecting consistent events.
submission.whats_next: We would add a level sharing gallery and improve the asset crop controls. We also want to make the analytics refresh handle small or empty datasets more gracefully.

submission.name: Spend Constellation
submission.tagline: See how everyday spending connects to the goals you care about.
submission.inspiration: We like visual tools that show relationships instead of forcing everything into fixed lists. We brought that idea to spending data for student clubs, where purchases for events, travel, and supplies can be hard to connect back to a budget.
submission.what_it_does: The app turns sample club transactions into a graph of purchases and categories, with larger spending shown as larger nodes. Databricks summarizes category patterns, Gemini drafts short explanations, and ElevenLabs can speak a selected insight; the voice option is a small add-on.
submission.how_we_built_it: A TypeScript and D3 frontend renders the graph, while a Go service parses CSV files and produces structured data. Python scripts send summaries to Databricks and Gemini, and an ElevenLabs call can turn one generated insight into audio.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The graph, analysis, and audio work in separate paths, and the demo can fail when a CSV has unexpected columns. We also found that category labels can make the visual hard to interpret when multiple club activities share similar purchases.
submission.accomplishments: We built an interactive graph from example financial records and showed how a club treasurer might inspect spending by category. We are pleased that the core visualization makes a familiar CSV feel easier to explore.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that data cleanup and labels shape the usefulness of a financial visualization as much as the chart itself. Gemini helped draft readable summaries, while the audio feature reminded us to keep spoken output short and tied to a specific item.
submission.whats_next: We would add saved budgets and a timeline to compare club spending across events. A later version could connect to approved account exports and make the analysis and narration more reliable.

submission.name: Storm Relay
submission.tagline: Give campus response teams a shared picture after severe weather.
submission.inspiration: Central Florida storms can leave students unsure where to report a problem or find help. We wanted to explore a shared map for campus volunteers and facilities staff to organize incoming reports during a weather event.
submission.what_it_does: A student can submit a short report that appears as a pin for a response coordinator, who can review reports and draft an area update. Gemini is used to summarize selected reports into a quick situation note; the live map and reporting flows are mockups and do not yet share state reliably.
submission.how_we_built_it: We started a React interface and a FastAPI service with REST endpoints for reports and messages. Gemini summarization is wired to a sample report path, while location sharing and the responder view currently use separate demo data.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Our biggest gap is that the reporting form, map, and responder tools are not connected end to end. We also ran out of time to check how reports from multiple people would be stored and updated during a real event.
submission.accomplishments: We created a clear prototype of the survivor report and responder review screens, and got a sample Gemini summary working. That gave us a concrete starting point for testing the workflow with real campus response partners later.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that emergency information needs to stay tied to its location and source, and that a useful summary cannot replace a reliable report pipeline. Gemini helped us condense sample messages, but the surrounding data flow needs more work.
submission.whats_next: We would connect reports to persistent geospatial storage and make map updates visible across users. We also want to add accessible voice reporting and test the workflow with campus response staff.

submission.name: Benefit Beacon
submission.tagline: A checkout-side guide to choosing a card for the purchase in front of you.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to help people make a more informed payment choice at the moment they shop, instead of expecting them to study card terms in advance. We focused on students and other new cardholders who may not know which benefits apply to a particular merchant.
submission.what_it_does: A browser extension recognizes likely checkout pages, estimates the merchant category, and suggests a matching card from a small wallet the user maintains in the dashboard. Users can compare rewards and basic fee or APR details, while a spoken summary makes the recommendation easier to catch during checkout.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used JavaScript, a Manifest V3 Chrome extension, and a Node.js/Express REST API to connect page signals to the user's saved cards. Merchant keywords and category rules drive the initial match, with Gemini helping rank ambiguous cases; the dashboard stores wallet details and the extension presents the result in a side panel.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Merchants structure checkout pages differently, and a URL or page label does not always reveal what is being purchased. Our category fallback can still be too broad, and recommendations depend on users entering accurate card terms and profile preferences.
submission.accomplishments: We connected checkout detection, merchant categorization, card matching, and a usable recommendation panel into one working flow. We are glad the prototype can show a relevant suggestion without asking someone to leave the checkout page.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that small errors in merchant classification can change a financial recommendation, so the reasoning and fallback behavior matter as much as the interface. Gemini helped us handle less familiar merchant descriptions, while building the extension taught us how much browser page variation affects detection.
submission.whats_next: We would like to test the extension across more merchants, make category matches easier for users to correct, and add clearer explanations of how each recommendation is calculated. A later version could explore transaction imports and spending summaries with appropriate account connections.

submission.name: Skillway Quest
submission.tagline: Turn a training handbook into a map of skills, missions, and quick checks.
submission.inspiration: New players and student club members often get a pile of guides without knowing which ideas they need before trying a more advanced task. We wanted to make learning a game-like path where each step helps explain what to practice next.
submission.what_it_does: Upload a game design or club training document and get an editable map of connected concepts, with small lessons, recall cards, and quizzes attached to its nodes. Gemini helps extract topics and generate the practice material, while progress marks show which missions a learner has completed.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a Next.js and React workspace with Supabase for sign-in, saved maps, and background processing of uploaded PDFs. Gemini turns document text into topic relationships and draft learning activities, and the interface lets learners explore the map and record progress between sessions.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Parsing PDFs into useful, connected concepts took iteration, and background jobs could get stuck or fail during upload processing. We added visible processing states and retries, though some documents still need a person to clean up the generated map.
submission.accomplishments: We got the upload-to-map workflow and the learning loop working together, including editable nodes, saved layouts, and progress tracking. The game-inspired missions gave us a way to make a course outline feel more like a set of achievable levels.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to treat AI-generated topics as drafts that need structure and review, and to design around asynchronous jobs so the interface does not imply work is finished too early. Gemini helped us prototype topic explanations and quizzes, while game design thinking helped shape progression and feedback.
submission.whats_next: We want to improve extraction on varied documents, add cooperative study missions, and let instructors share curated maps. We would also like to tune the difficulty of activities based on learner progress.

submission.name: Bench Breaker
submission.tagline: A little desk-side accountability for campus makers finishing a work session.
submission.inspiration: In a shared workshop, it is easy to wander from a build task into checking a phone, especially when a deadline is close. We wanted a physical reminder that could make a short work block feel more engaging without needing someone else to keep watch.
submission.what_it_does: A webcam checks for phone use during a timed work session, and Gemini confirms likely distractions before generating a short spoken nudge through ElevenLabs. An Arduino controls a small indicator and a brief air puff toward a desk target, giving the reminder a physical cue; Databricks records session events for a simple view of when interruptions happen.
submission.how_we_built_it: A Python and OpenCV loop runs YOLOv8 phone detection on a laptop and sends likely events to Gemini for a quick confirmation and message. ElevenLabs turns that text into audio, while the laptop sends a signal to an Arduino relay that powers a small pump; session events are written to a Databricks table so we can inspect patterns afterward.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The camera, model calls, audio playback, Arduino control, and event logging each worked, but keeping them coordinated without delays took most of our time. The detection can mistake a phone-shaped object for a phone, and network lag sometimes makes the spoken cue arrive after the moment has passed; the air puff is also intentionally small and aimed only at a test target.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a live vision loop to both spoken feedback and a physical response, and got the session log flowing into Databricks. We are proud that the project feels tangible at a desk rather than being only another timer window.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much timing and hardware safety matter when software triggers a physical device, and why audio should not interrupt the user's work unpredictably. ElevenLabs made the feedback feel more expressive, Gemini helped vary the wording, and Databricks gave us a first look at turning session events into a useful summary.
submission.whats_next: We would like to add user-controlled sensitivity, quieter notification options, and better handling for different desk layouts. We also want to make the event summaries clearer and let users review or delete their session history.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides central audio interaction for work session reminders, but integration challenges and limitations affect functionality.

submission.tagline: A camera-guided rover that can spot obstacles and mark a safer route through a workshop.
submission.inspiration: Busy workshops and maker spaces can have cluttered aisles that are hard to inspect from the entrance. We wanted to prototype a small mobile scout that could help a student or staff member notice blocked paths before carrying equipment through them.
submission.what_it_does: A camera feed is analyzed for a few common obstacle types, and the system points a small servo-mounted marker toward the detected area while a wheeled base moves through a test lane. Gemini can turn a detection summary into a short plain-language note, but a person still decides whether the route is safe to use.
submission.how_we_built_it: A Jetson runs Python, OpenCV, and a YOLO model on the camera feed to estimate where an obstacle appears in the frame. It sends compact direction commands over a local network to a laptop, which relays them by serial connection to an Arduino controlling the wheels, servo, and indicator; Gemini receives only the summarized detection so it can produce a readable note for the operator.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The camera angle and lighting changed detection quality, and noisy coordinates made the marker twitch until we smoothed its movement. Network delay between the Jetson, laptop, and Arduino sometimes made the rover react late, so it can still bump into objects during quick turns; we kept the test area slow and supervised.
submission.accomplishments: We connected edge vision, networked control, and a physical rover into an end-to-end demonstration. We are proud that the marker and short Gemini note give the operator two ways to understand what the camera noticed.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a detection model is only one part of a useful robot: camera placement, command timing, and motor response all shape the result. Gemini was useful for turning a small amount of structured output into a readable note, but it does not verify the scene or make a safety decision.
submission.whats_next: We would like to improve obstacle detection across lighting conditions, add an emergency stop and more reliable distance sensing, and test the route marking with a larger set of workshop layouts. We would also explore whether the notes could be saved for facilities staff to review later.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini provides a meaningful secondary function by converting detection summaries into notes, but is not central to the rover's core navigation.

submission.name: Campus Voice Desk
submission.tagline: A voice led incident helper for student IT teams trying to sort out a late night outage.
submission.inspiration: When a campus service breaks after hours, the person who notices may not know what information the IT team needs first. We wanted to try a phone friendly way to capture the report and turn it into a clear first pass for whoever is on call.
submission.what_it_does: A user can send a short voice report or text description of an IT issue, and the prototype turns it into a spoken summary with suggested triage questions. We planned a set of specialist analysis steps, but the voice intake, analysis, and response are not connected end to end yet.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Python and FastAPI for a small backend, with a basic web interface for submitting reports. ElevenLabs generates the spoken response; separate agent-style analysis experiments can inspect a report, but they are not yet orchestrated into the same flow.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The main failure was integration: the audio response and the analysis pieces run separately, so the full incident path does not reliably complete in the demo. We also had to keep the spoken output short enough to be useful during a busy support shift.
submission.accomplishments: We have a working voice response for sample IT reports and a rough interface for submitting one. The project gave us a concrete way to explore how natural audio might help a small support team gather useful details.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that voice interaction needs careful pacing and concise prompts, especially when someone is reporting a problem. Using ElevenLabs helped us test a more human sounding response, while our data experiments showed how much work remains to connect separate components reliably.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the report intake, analysis, and audio response in one tested flow. We would also add a way for a human support lead to review and edit the suggested summary before it is shared.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is central to the voice response but integration is incomplete.

submission.name: Study Sprout
submission.tagline: Keep a little study buddy growing as your group works through its weekly tasks.
submission.inspiration: Our team wanted to make recurring study tasks feel less like a plain checklist, especially for students working together in a small course group. A small character seemed like a fun way to show progress without adding another complicated study planner.
submission.what_it_does: Students can add study tasks, mark them complete, and earn coins that help a plant-like companion grow. The app also shows a shared group progress view; the shop is a simple version with a limited set of decorations.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a browser interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, plus a FastAPI backend in Python that stores task and companion data in JSON. The frontend sends updates through the API and refreshes the group view after changes.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Combining separate frontend pieces and settling on a consistent data shape took time. The app works through the main flow, but rapid updates from multiple students can sometimes leave the displayed group totals stale until a refresh.
submission.accomplishments: We made the task-to-reward loop work from the browser through the backend, and drew the companion art ourselves. We are proud that the basic group view and character state survive a page reload.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to agree on API shapes earlier and to keep features modular enough to change. We also saw how quickly a small shared-state feature can expose timing issues in a web app.
submission.whats_next: We would add more companion variations and a better decoration shop. We would also improve live updates and try a course platform connection if an appropriate API is available.

challenge_results.rationale: A simple plant companion for study tasks shows some originality but uses common web tech.

submission.name: KiteWatch
submission.tagline: A family browser companion that flags concerning pages and gives teens a calm voice prompt.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to explore how families could talk about troubling online material without making every browsing session feel watched. We focused on a shared household computer, where a brief supportive prompt might help a teen pause and ask for help.
submission.what_it_does: A Chrome extension periodically checks the active page and asks Gemini to classify a screenshot into a few safety categories. When a page crosses the alert threshold, the extension can show a gentle on-screen message and play a short ElevenLabs voice prompt; safe images are discarded, and the prototype does not send parent emails.
submission.how_we_built_it: The extension uses TypeScript and Chrome APIs to capture and process screenshots, then sends them to a small server for Gemini classification. A React dashboard shows device and alert status, while a category-specific message is sent to ElevenLabs for playback; Databricks was used for a small exploration of aggregate sample classifications, not the live decision path.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Screenshots can be ambiguous, and the classifier sometimes returns inconsistent labels, so the alert threshold needs more work. Coordinating extension permissions, server responses, and audio playback also took careful debugging.
submission.accomplishments: We connected page capture, classification, an alert overlay, and a spoken message into a working prototype. We also designed the flow to discard pages classified as safe rather than keeping a browsing history.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that privacy expectations need to shape the data flow from the start, and that an AI label should be treated as a prompt for a conversation rather than a final judgment. ElevenLabs made the messages feel less like system alerts, and our Databricks experiment introduced us to examining classification patterns in aggregate.
submission.whats_next: We would test the experience with families, add more control over alert categories, and improve handling for video and page text. We would also make the dashboard clearer about what gets processed and retained.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used for a minor exploratory analysis of aggregate classifications, not the live decision path, limiting relevance.

submission.name: GrantGraph
submission.tagline: Map research citations and spot funding topics that may be gaining momentum.
submission.inspiration: We wanted research teams to see how papers connect while getting a quick sense of which themes might be worth exploring next. We combined citation mapping with a simple opportunity view inspired by comparing prices across a changing market.
submission.what_it_does: Users add research paper links to a shared workspace, where the app builds a citation graph and highlights frequently referenced papers that are missing from the collection. Gemini summarizes topic clusters and compares their recent paper counts to flag areas with changing activity; Databricks handles a small aggregate analysis of sample metadata.
submission.how_we_built_it: The app uses React and React Flow with a FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL, and Semantic Scholar metadata. Gemini powers grounded summaries, while a Databricks notebook prepares sample publication data for the trend panel; the team graph, gap list, and chat flow work through the demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Paper metadata varies, and graph gaps can be confusing when a suggested citation is later added. We also had to explain that a rise in paper counts is only a signal to investigate, not evidence that a topic will receive funding.
submission.accomplishments: We connected paper ingestion to a shared graph, missing-citation suggestions, and a cited chat view. We also got a small data trend panel working alongside the research workflow.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that useful research assistance depends on showing where an answer came from and labeling uncertain signals clearly. Gemini helped summarize the workspace, while the market comparison idea pushed us to think about changes over time instead of a static list.
submission.whats_next: We would improve membership checks and add citation exports. We would also validate the trend view against broader publication data and make its limits more visible.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini is central for summarizing topic clusters and comparing trends, but the core citation graph and gap detection work without it.

submission.name: Ledger Lantern
submission.tagline: Spot unusual account activity and hear a quick explanation of what stood out.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make transaction review less intimidating for people who help manage finances at neighborhood nonprofits. Small teams may not have time to inspect every line in a statement, even when catching an unfamiliar charge matters.
submission.what_it_does: Ledger Lantern compares recent transactions with a simple history of typical amounts and flags entries that cross a configurable threshold. A short ElevenLabs voice readout describes the flagged item so a staff member can review it while working through the list.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Python to calculate transaction patterns and SQL to store and query sample account activity, with a small API and Streamlit screen for uploading and viewing data. We planned the voice feature around ElevenLabs, but it is only loosely connected to the review flow in this demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Choosing thresholds that catch unusual charges without producing too many false alarms was difficult, and our test data was too small to tune them well. The separate data and interface pieces run, but we did not get the complete upload-to-alert experience working reliably end to end.
submission.accomplishments: We put together a basic transaction review screen and a first pass at comparing activity against historical averages. We are glad we kept the scope focused enough to show how a small finance team might triage a statement.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much transaction formats affect even simple analysis, and how Python and SQL can work together for a review tool. AI coding assistance helped us sketch the UI and voice-readout integration, but we still had to debug the data flow by hand.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the upload, flagging, and spoken summary into one dependable path, then let staff tune thresholds for different account types. We would also add clear review and dismissal notes so a flag is treated as a prompt for human checking, not a fraud verdict.

challenge_results.rationale: Ledger Lantern addresses a meaningful financial process improvement with a focused scope on transaction review for nonprofits, using Python and SQL for analysis and a voice readout for accessibility.

submission.name: AidStatement
submission.tagline: Turn scattered scholarship and student aid documents into a clearer funding picture.
submission.inspiration: Students often receive aid details in different statements and notices, making it hard to see what is due and when. We wanted to adapt document parsing and financial summaries into a tool for student support offices helping people organize those records.
submission.what_it_does: AidStatement is a prototype for uploading aid letters, expense CSVs, and receipt images, then extracting dates and amounts into a single view. A Gemini-powered summary is meant to explain the entries in plain language, with ElevenLabs reading the summary aloud; several of these pieces are currently demos rather than a connected workflow.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and TypeScript frontend with a Node and Express backend, styled with Tailwind and charted with Recharts. Gemini handles planned document and CSV interpretation, MongoDB is set up for persistence, and we prototyped spoken summaries with ElevenLabs, but the components do not yet share a complete data path.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Aid letters and receipts vary a lot, so extracting reliable dates and totals from them took more time than expected. Authentication, storage, parsing, and audio were built as separate parts, and the live upload-to-summary flow is still mocked in places.
submission.accomplishments: We built a responsive dashboard concept that brings aid items and expenses into one place and explored parsing more than one document format. The prototype gives us a concrete starting point for a student finance workflow.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that document parsing needs checks against the original source before anyone acts on a result. Gemini helped us explore extraction and summaries, while the ElevenLabs experiment showed us how spoken explanations could help students review complex notices.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the upload, extraction, review, and spoken explanation steps, then add source highlights beside each extracted amount. We would also test with varied sample documents and improve sign-in and data handling before considering real student records.

challenge_results.rationale: AidStatement addresses a meaningful student financial process by integrating document parsing and summaries but lacks a connected workflow.

submission.name: AidCall Drill
submission.tagline: Practice the first few minutes of a campus emergency response through voice-led scenarios.
submission.inspiration: On a large campus, a student or staff member may have to report an incident before they know which details responders need. We wanted to turn emergency guidance into a short decision game, and borrowed the idea of a voice front desk that gathers context and routes urgent information for review.
submission.what_it_does: The player works through a simulated campus incident, choosing actions as new details arrive and answering a Gemini dispatcher that asks follow-up questions. At the end, the app creates a brief report and reads key points aloud; the experience works from start to finish, though dispatcher responses sometimes repeat or lag.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built the scenario interface in React with Tailwind, and used Gemini to generate context-aware dispatcher prompts and a closing review from the player's choices. Browser speech input captures replies and Google Cloud Text-to-Speech voices the dispatcher, while a simple campus map model uses locations and connections to shape available actions.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Keeping the voice exchange aligned with the game state was unreliable, and the dispatcher can repeat a prompt or miss part of an answer. Our campus locations are a small modeled set, so the route choices are not a live map or a substitute for official emergency procedures.
submission.accomplishments: We connected scenario choices, a contextual dispatcher, and a spoken wrap-up into a playable emergency practice loop. We are proud that Gemini can use the player's current situation to make the conversation feel tied to the exercise.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to give a language model constrained context when its answer needs to match a game state, and saw how much timing matters in a voice interface. The voice-front-desk pattern also helped us think about collecting useful details before routing an incident for human review.
submission.whats_next: We would make turn-taking more reliable, add more campus scenarios, and review the guidance with university emergency staff. A future version could let teams coordinate roles during a drill and produce a clearer handoff report.

challenge_results.rationale: The project improves emergency response training with voice interaction but is not directly related to financial services processes.

submission.name: Shift Memory
submission.tagline: A wearable note taker that helps student workers recall where equipment and handoff details came up.
submission.inspiration: Student workers move between counters, labs, and event spaces, then need to remember where a tool was left or what a teammate said during a busy shift. We wanted to explore a wearable capture-and-search tool for those moments, while keeping the user in control of what gets saved.
submission.what_it_does: A glasses-mounted camera and microphone feed sample visual and audio moments into a searchable timeline, where users can ask questions and hear a generated response through ElevenLabs. Gemini is used to describe selected scenes, and we added a simple tag for marking a moment as relevant to a shift handoff; the capture, search, and response pieces are not fully connected yet.
submission.how_we_built_it: Two ESP32 boards prototype camera and microphone capture, with a Python backend handling frame selection, transcription, and storage in SQLite and ChromaDB. Gemini creates scene descriptions and answers searches, while a Next.js and TypeScript interface shows saved moments and uses ElevenLabs for speech; the live hardware stream and UI still rely on separate pieces.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Keeping the camera and microphone streams stable over WiFi took repeated debugging, and audio sample conversion produced inconsistent results. We also ran into API limits and database write coordination, so we mocked parts of the memory search instead of completing a dependable live pipeline.
submission.accomplishments: We got the wearable capture hardware sending data and built separate prototypes for scene descriptions, semantic search, and spoken replies. We are proud of the pieces we explored, even though they do not yet behave as one finished assistant.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned the basics of ESP32 camera streaming, audio capture, and vector search, along with the practical limits of real-time AI calls. Gemini helped us prototype scene summaries, and ElevenLabs made the idea of hands-free spoken recall tangible.
submission.whats_next: We would stabilize streaming and connect saved moments to search and spoken playback before adding more features. A next iteration should make recording visible and easy to pause, and let workers explicitly review what is retained for handoffs.

submission.name: Fieldnote Voice
submission.tagline: Turn campus garden logs into quick, spoken care reminders.
submission.inspiration: Campus garden volunteers share plots and rotate watering, but notes about what was planted or tended can be scattered across notebooks. We wanted a lightweight way for student garden teams to turn those observations into an easier handoff.
submission.what_it_does: Users can upload a CSV of garden observations and ask questions about recent watering or plant care; Gemini drafts a short summary, and ElevenLabs can read it aloud. The end-to-end demo works inconsistently because date and plant names in the sample files are not always parsed correctly.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made a small HTML and JavaScript interface for CSV upload and audio playback, backed by Python and Flask for parsing and API calls. Gemini generates care summaries from the parsed rows, while ElevenLabs converts the response into speech.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: CSV columns and handwritten-style abbreviations are easy to misread, which can make a reminder incomplete. We also had trouble keeping the upload, summary, and audio steps reliable in one session.
submission.accomplishments: We built a working prototype that can turn a garden log into a short spoken summary. It gave us a useful starting point for making volunteer handoffs easier to scan.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to validate the input data before asking Gemini to summarize it, and got practical experience connecting Flask with two APIs.
submission.whats_next: We would add a review step for uncertain entries and support shared plot notes across volunteers. We would also test more CSV layouts and make reminders configurable by plant and schedule.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini is central to generating care summaries from garden logs, but inconsistent parsing and reliability issues limit functionality.

submission.name: Quiet Quench
submission.tagline: A spoken nudge and splash for campus study sessions that keep getting interrupted.
submission.inspiration: We built this for students trying to study in busy dorms and shared apartments, where a phone break can turn into a long detour. We wanted a physical reminder that makes the interruption hard to ignore, with a voice that can call out the moment too.
submission.what_it_does: A webcam and YOLOv8 watch for a phone being picked up during a study session. When one appears, the app asks Gemini to check the image and come up with a short teasing line, then ElevenLabs reads it aloud while an Arduino switches on a small water pump.
submission.how_we_built_it: Python and OpenCV handle the webcam feed and YOLOv8 detection, while separate threads keep video capture moving during API requests. Gemini checks a detected phone and supplies the message; ElevenLabs turns that text into speech. An Arduino and relay control the pump when the laptop sends a trigger.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We planned to run the vision code on a Raspberry Pi, but the boards we had could not be brought up reliably. We moved the detection work to a laptop and used the Arduino for the pump, so the demo works but depends on the laptop staying connected and the camera seeing the desk.
submission.accomplishments: We got the camera detection, generated voice, and physical pump working together for a study-session demo. Adding a short pen tip to the outlet made the water stream more noticeable, and threading helped avoid freezing the camera while waiting for responses.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to wire a relay and microcontroller to a physical output, and how much time hardware setup can take. We also got practice with YOLOv8, concurrent tasks, and shaping text so a synthesized voice sounds like a quick interruption rather than a long announcement.
submission.whats_next: We would like to add a way to follow a student who moves away from the camera's view, and make the pump trigger safer to use around study materials. A more reliable single-board setup would also make it easier to move between desks.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is central to the study interruption response, but hardware limitations and laptop dependency reduce functionality.

submission.name: Page Harbor
submission.tagline: A browser companion that spots risky advice in student job and housing searches.
submission.inspiration: Students often search for housing, work, and local services without knowing which pages are trustworthy. We wanted to make a small browser tool that can flag concerning material while showing only a limited alert instead of keeping a record of ordinary browsing.
submission.what_it_does: A Chrome extension periodically captures the active tab and sends an image to a backend for Gemini classification into safe, review, or harmful categories. The prototype can show an alert in the browser and speak a brief, supportive explanation using ElevenLabs; safe captures are discarded, and repeated similar alerts are suppressed. A basic React dashboard is intended to show flagged items and device settings.
submission.how_we_built_it: The TypeScript Manifest V3 extension uses a background service worker to capture tabs, preprocess images, and send them to a Fastify server. The server calls Gemini Vision for a category and confidence, then applies a threshold and cooldown before deciding whether to alert; it uses ElevenLabs to generate the spoken prompt. MongoDB stores device and alert records, while a React dashboard reads those records and provides basic management controls. These pieces connect through typed request and response shapes shared with Zod.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Gemini results were not always consistent, and rate limits and malformed responses made the classification path unreliable. Our fallback can mark an uncertain result for review, but that does not guarantee the right category. The dashboard, extension, and server each run, though the full device-registration and alert flow still needs more end-to-end hardening.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a browser capture flow to an image classifier and a child-facing alert with both visual and spoken feedback. We also added deduplication and cooldown logic so a page that remains open does not immediately generate the same notification over and over.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how Chrome service workers, alarms, and content scripts coordinate, and how much validation an AI response needs before it can drive an alert. Gemini helped us sketch classification prompts and response handling, but we still had to test edge cases and account for model failures ourselves. ElevenLabs made the alerts easier to hear without building a recording pipeline.
submission.whats_next: We would like to test the classification flow on more kinds of student-facing pages and tune the categories with families and student support staff. We also want to finish device enrollment, improve dashboard settings, and make alert language configurable by age and context.

challenge_results.rationale: The project uses Gemini centrally for image classification into safety categories but faces reliability issues; the integration is meaningful but not yet fully robust.

submission.name: Campus Cadence
submission.tagline: A compact ride display for campus couriers, with a weekly distance board.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make a simple ride readout for students who bike between campus buildings to deliver club materials or help with events. A weekly distance board seemed like a fun way for small volunteer crews to compare how much ground they cover.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype reads location data to estimate a rider's speed and distance, then presents the ride on a small display. A companion website is meant to collect weekly totals for a crew leaderboard; the map view is a separate demonstration of the location data.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used an ESP32 with a GPS module and Arduino-style C++ code to calculate speed and mileage from successive positions. When the module struggled to get a fix, we also tried passing phone location data to the board. The display, website, and map each have working pieces, but ride data is not yet reliably connected to the leaderboard.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The GPS receiver took a long time to lock onto satellites, so location and speed readings were inconsistent. We also designed the case before accounting for space for a battery and button, then had to modify the print by hand.
submission.accomplishments: We worked out the basic distance and speed calculations and built a compact display concept around them. We also made a first pass at a map and weekly comparison page, though those parts still need a dependable shared data flow.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that GPS location quality changes a lot with the environment and that using a phone as a location source brings its own connection work. The hardware packaging also taught us to plan for the battery and controls before printing an enclosure.
submission.whats_next: Next we would improve GPS reception, connect each ride to the website automatically, and add a more personalized display. An optional gyroscope could estimate incline for riders who want more detail about their route.

challenge_results.rationale: The project shows a clear concept with some working components but lacks reliable data flow and detailed technical explanations.

submission.name: SkillScroll
submission.tagline: A short-form learning feed where campus clubs share practical how-to clips.
submission.inspiration: Student organizations often teach useful skills informally, but their advice can get buried in chat threads or long documents. We wanted to try a swipeable feed where club members can share short explainers and viewers can find clips by topic.
submission.what_it_does: The web prototype presents short educational clips with topic labels and a basic feed. A sentence-transformer check can compare a transcript with a selected topic, and the design includes a points display for engagement. Upload validation, the feed, and reward tracking currently work as separate pieces; points are only a demo and no token transfers are connected.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made the interface with React, TypeScript, and Vite, with a FastAPI backend for clip and transcript endpoints. Sentence Transformers provide a relevance score for a transcript, while MongoDB is intended to keep users, clips, and engagement data together. We also sketched a Solana reward flow, but the wallet and on-chain pieces are not wired into the prototype, so the UI shows sample reward states.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Video upload and playback took more time than expected, and our relevance check can be slow on longer transcripts. The feed, model check, and reward mock are not yet connected into one complete publishing flow, so a clip can appear without its points reflecting a real transaction.
submission.accomplishments: We built a usable feed interface and got a first semantic topic check running against clip text. We also mapped out how a club learning feed might use engagement points without claiming that a real token economy is ready.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that an embedding similarity score is a rough relevance signal, not a guarantee that advice is useful or correct. Building a familiar scrolling interface was easier than coordinating media storage, model processing, and rewards into one path.
submission.whats_next: We would connect uploads, transcript checks, and the feed through a background job, then test the flow with a small set of club tutorials. If that works, we could explore non-crypto badges or a real reward system with clearer abuse protections.

submission.name: GrantRoute
submission.tagline: A quick guide to the next step when a small organization handles a payment.
submission.inspiration: Student clubs and neighborhood groups often make purchases with limited budgets and confusing payment options. We wanted to help a treasurer quickly compare likely benefits and keep a short explanation beside the decision.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype lets a user choose a purchase category and compare example cards or payment methods against a small rewards table. Gemini can turn the comparison into a plain-language summary, and ElevenLabs can read that summary aloud. Account linking and recommendations are still mocked, so the demo uses sample organization profiles and card data.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and Next.js interface with a small backend that looks up reward rules from JSON data. A Gemini request drafts a short explanation from the selected category and matching rates, while ElevenLabs converts the explanation to speech. Plaid Sandbox account retrieval was explored separately, but it is not connected to the recommendation flow yet.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting reliable location or merchant context proved difficult, and our example reward rules cover only a narrow set of cards. The account connection and recommendation pieces are not joined, so a user still has to choose from sample data rather than their actual accounts.
submission.accomplishments: We made a compact comparison screen and demonstrated a spoken explanation of why one sample option might fit a purchase. The prototype focuses on making the decision understandable for a group treasurer rather than only showing a multiplier.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that an apparent reward rate is only useful when the merchant category and card rules line up. AI can make a comparison easier to explain, but it cannot fix missing or stale rewards data.
submission.whats_next: We would connect account retrieval, expand the rules database, and let organizations save purchase policies for future treasurers. We would also add clearer checks for fees and other conditions before presenting a recommendation.

submission.name: Pocket Portfolio Lab
submission.tagline: Build a paper trading rule and see what market signals it reacts to.
submission.inspiration: We were interested in quantitative finance but found that the tools used to explore trading rules often assume a lot of math and market knowledge. We wanted a browser prototype where student finance clubs could assemble a simple paper strategy and inspect the signals behind it.
submission.what_it_does: Users connect visual blocks to define a paper trading rule, such as reacting to a moving average or a news sentiment signal. The app collects available market headlines and price data, shows the selected signals, and simulates the rule against a ticker without placing real trades. Gemini explains the rule and its inputs in plain language so a beginner can understand what the blocks are asking the simulator to do.
submission.how_we_built_it: The interface uses Blockly with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS to let users assemble conditions without writing Python. A Python backend turns those blocks into a constrained strategy format, requests price and news data, and stores strategy runs in SQL. The BNY angle is an educational workflow for understanding investment decision inputs; it is not connected to bank accounts or brokerage execution. Gemini receives the strategy description and displayed signals to produce an explanation, while the simulation remains a separate deterministic step.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting Blockly’s generated logic into a form our Python service could safely interpret took time, and its documentation left us guessing in places. Sentiment from short posts and headlines can be noisy, and our data model for keeping prices, headlines, and run settings together still needs work. The prototype’s market data coverage is limited, so its output should be treated as an exercise rather than investment guidance.
submission.accomplishments: We connected the visual editor to a backend simulation path and can inspect how a paper rule responds to the data we fetch. We are proud that the explanations make the block configuration less intimidating without hiding the underlying inputs.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to map a visual program into a constrained backend representation and how much detail matters when explaining financial indicators. Gemini was useful for turning a strategy description into beginner-friendly language, but we had to keep its explanation tied to the values the simulator actually displayed. We also got more comfortable combining API collection with SQL records for repeatable runs.
submission.whats_next: We would add more block types, improve the history and comparison views, and make the data refresh path more reliable. A future version could test additional public signals and let instructors share example strategies with a class.

submission.name: Campus Momentum
submission.tagline: Build steady habits around class, wellbeing, and your money.
submission.inspiration: We wanted a lightweight way for students to keep track of small goals without juggling separate habit and spending apps. Campus Momentum turns a few daily choices into progress for a personal character.
submission.what_it_does: Students log habits and selected spending decisions to earn or lose experience, review a short progress history, and get suggested next steps. Gemini helps tailor the suggestions, and ElevenLabs reads level-up and task-completion prompts aloud.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used TypeScript and JavaScript for the app, with Capital One data represented by a limited sample connection and Gemini used to rank suggested quests and spending categories. ElevenLabs generates short audio cues when progress changes. The main screens and APIs connect, but the finance sync sometimes fails and a few transaction examples are still mocked.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the shared app structure and API calls to work together took several rounds of cleanup. We also had to adjust Gemini prompts so task suggestions matched their intended difficulty, and the spending flow can still show stale data after a failed sync.
submission.accomplishments: We connected habit tracking, a progress system, and voice feedback into one student-focused prototype. We are glad the app can show a useful path through the main flow even though some data handling remains unreliable.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to coordinate work across a shared codebase and to treat prompt design as part of the product logic. ElevenLabs made progress cues easy to hear, while Gemini helped shape suggestions from the user’s goals.
submission.whats_next: We would make transaction syncing more dependable, add clearer controls for financial data, and let users record reflections by voice or video. Shared progress with friends could also be explored later.

submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and TypeScript frontend with Leaflet for the map, and an Express backend with MongoDB and Mongoose for resource records. submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to connect Leaflet interactions with stored coordinates and how to shape MongoDB queries for a simple search experience. Gemini was a small experiment in reducing form typing, rather than a required part of finding a location.
submission.whats_next: We would improve address validation, make deployment stable, and add clearer ways to confirm that a listed repair resource is still available. Community updates and login could come after that.

submission.name: Molecule Habit Garden
submission.tagline: Grow a routine by turning small goals into building blocks.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make personal goals feel easier to start by connecting daily habits with a visual sense of progress. A second idea came from molecule tools that turn a compact text description into a possible sequence of components.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype lets users choose a goal, log a few daily tasks, and see a small progress garden change as they keep going. A separate mocked screen accepts a molecule-style string and displays a sample sequence of habit steps, but it is not connected to the goal tracker.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React Native for the task and reflection screens, Express with Supabase for user progress, and a Cohere-powered coach concept for guidance. submission.name: FieldGuide Lens
submission.tagline: A first-pass visual guide to plant problems for community garden volunteers.
submission.inspiration: Community garden volunteers often have to decide what to do when a leaf or fruit looks unhealthy, but expert help may not be nearby. We wanted to make a phone-based reference that turns a photo and a few observations into clearer questions to bring to a local grower.
submission.what_it_does: The app lets a volunteer note the plant type, where the issue appears, and how long it has been visible, then take a guided photo. A sample image classifier is intended to suggest possible plant issues, while Gemini can combine that label with the answers into a plain-language summary and suggested next steps. It is a prototype for learning and triage, not an authoritative diagnosis, and the classifier and summary are not yet connected in the demo.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made the interface in React Native with Expo and TypeScript, using a camera guide to encourage a closer, well-lit photo. A Hugging Face image model is the planned source of candidate labels, and Gemini is meant to explain those labels alongside the volunteer's notes. The reason for splitting the work this way is to give the image model a narrow classification job and let Gemini handle the contextual explanation. During the weekend, the mobile flow and AI experiments worked separately, so results still need a reliable handoff between them.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Photo quality changed a lot with distance, shadows, and phone cameras, which made a single image hard to interpret consistently. We also spent time trying to make Gemini's wording useful without making a guess sound certain. Several screens and model calls remained disconnected, and merging changes between branches cost time.
submission.accomplishments: We built a working mobile shell with a guided capture flow and a place to show a contextual result. We are glad we narrowed the project to one practical garden question instead of trying to cover every plant or condition.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how image classification and language models can serve different roles in a small app, and why passing structured information between them matters. Gemini helped us draft explanations, but we had to keep the output cautious and reviewable. We also got more practice optimizing photos and coordinating mobile work across branches.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the classifier output to the Gemini prompt and save prior observations so volunteers can compare changes over time. We would also want input from experienced growers and more varied plant photos before treating any suggestions as dependable.

challenge_results.rationale: The app addresses plant health identification for community gardens using image classification and Gemini explanations, but finance is only a side concern for volunteer workflow improvement.

submission.name: Garden Signs
submission.tagline: Show a garden sign, get a clearer way to share what you need.
submission.inspiration: Volunteers at a community garden may not share a first language, and simple signs or instructions can be hard to communicate quickly. We wanted to combine a local garden resource map with a camera tool that recognizes a few hand-spelled letters, so people can find useful places and share short labels.
submission.what_it_does: The map prototype collects nearby gardens, public growing spaces, and selected community resources from open listings. A separate webcam experiment tries to recognize ASL fingerspelling and display the detected letters as text. We pictured using that to search or label a map marker, but the two parts are not connected yet and the gesture model is limited to individual letters.
submission.how_we_built_it: The map interface uses React, Vite, Tailwind, and Leaflet, with a small FastAPI service and SQLite for saved markers. OpenStreetMap data and a few public resource sources provide starting locations, while Gemini can draft short descriptions from available listing details. For the second interaction, we built a browser camera experiment that classifies hand shapes and groups recognized letters into text. The map and camera tools run as separate prototypes; connecting recognized words to map search is the next integration step.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Listings from different sources use inconsistent categories and can be out of date, so a combined map can still mislead. Webcam recognition also depends on framing and lighting, and letter-by-letter output is slow for real conversation. We did not have time to link the camera results to the map or test the flow with garden volunteers.
submission.accomplishments: We are proud to have two concrete pieces: a map with several kinds of community locations and a small fingerspelling recognition demo. Working on both showed us how a communication aid could fit into a practical local-resource tool.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned the tradeoffs involved in combining open map data with manually saved locations, and how much visual input conditions affect a webcam classifier. Gemini helped draft concise listing descriptions, while our camera experiment taught us that recognition needs a clear task and good framing. We also learned that separate prototypes need a shared data shape before they can feel like one app.
submission.whats_next: We would connect recognized letters to a simple place search or marker label, then improve recognition for short words. We would also add a way for garden groups to correct listings and flag outdated information.

submission.name: ClubTab
submission.tagline: A simple money dashboard for student club treasurers.
submission.inspiration: Student organizations often have several people trying to understand the same small budget, and transaction lists can be difficult to explain at a glance. We wanted to make a lightweight place where a treasurer could see recent activity and ask basic questions about club spending.
submission.what_it_does: ClubTab shows a sample club account's purchases, deposits, and withdrawals, with a chart grouping spending into a few categories. A chat helper explains common banking and budget terms in plain language. The account feed and assistant are separate in this prototype, so the assistant does not yet answer questions using the displayed transactions.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the dashboard, and Python with Flask for account and API work. The original plan was to use a financial-data API for transaction records and an LLM endpoint for the helper's explanations. Those pieces connect through the Flask layer in the intended design, while the current demo relies on sample account data and a standalone assistant prompt. We focused the interface on a club treasurer's view rather than building a general personal finance product.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the account data, chart, and assistant to share the same information was harder than building each screen on its own. We also lost time sorting out Git merges, and the financial API flow is represented with sample data rather than a complete live connection.
submission.accomplishments: We made a usable dashboard layout with a transaction list and a spending breakdown, and we sketched how a treasurer could get plain-language help from the same site. This was our first time bringing a finance-oriented API concept and a web app together in a weekend.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned more about organizing frontend and Flask work, and about the work involved in moving financial records safely into a user-facing screen. The AI helper showed us how an LLM can explain terms, but it needs account context before it can give useful answers.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the chat helper to selected account summaries and make the categories editable for each club. We would also replace sample transactions with a dependable financial data integration and add support for multiple club accounts.

challenge_results.rationale: ClubTab addresses a meaningful improvement to a student club financial process with a dashboard and chat helper, but the chat functionality is disconnected from transaction data and uses sample data.

submission.name: Nest Egg Quest
submission.tagline: A small-choice money game about building a cushion before life gets expensive.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make money planning feel less intimidating for students starting out on their own. We focused on how everyday choices can affect the ability to handle later costs, rather than treating finance as a lecture.
submission.what_it_does: Players move through short life scenarios and choose how to use a limited budget, with a simple view of how saving decisions change their future cushion. Gemini can suggest a follow-up scenario or give a brief explanation of a choice. A Databricks notebook was meant to summarize scenario outcomes, while the BNY angle is the budgeting decision itself.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React, Vite, and Tailwind for the game screens, with Node and MongoDB planned for saving progress. Gemini was wired in for scenario text, and we tried a small Databricks analysis of the game’s sample outcomes. The pieces run separately, but the full loop from a player choice through saved data and analysis is not connected yet; the ElevenLabs narration was also only a stub.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We had more ideas than we could connect in the time available, especially around saving player state and making the scenarios feel varied. The demo does not work end-to-end: the game screens and some integrations can be shown in isolation, but choices do not reliably flow through persistence and the analysis view. We also did not finish the spoken guidance.
submission.accomplishments: We made a playable-looking set of money decision screens and got the core scenario idea into a form we could demonstrate. We are proud that the project stays approachable and gives the player a way to compare choices without involving real money.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how quickly game state can get tangled when screens, scenario data, and persistence are developed in parallel. Gemini helped us draft alternate scenario wording, but we still had to constrain it so the choices stayed understandable and usable in the game.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the choice flow to saved sessions and make the results view update reliably. We also want to finish the narrated prompts and give the Databricks analysis a clearer role in showing which decisions change the simulated cushion.

challenge_results.rationale: The submission improves financial literacy through a game-based approach but lacks end-to-end functionality and deeper technical explanations.

submission.name: ReadyCheck Voice
submission.tagline: Practice checking safety gear before a campus event shift
submission.inspiration: Student volunteers and event crews sometimes take on unfamiliar setup jobs where protective gear matters. We wanted a quick practice tool that can check a few visible items and explain what might be missing.
submission.what_it_does: ReadyCheck Voice lets a user choose a sample event scenario, then uses a camera view to look for items such as gloves, goggles, or a vest. It gives a spoken status and can play through a short training scenario; it is a prototype for practice, not an operational safety check.
submission.how_we_built_it: The app combines a FastAPI backend with a React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind interface. A YOLO11n model handles image detection, Gemini can draft scenario variations, and ElevenLabs voices the feedback; we also tried organizing example detection records in Databricks for later review.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The demo connects the camera, detection, and spoken feedback paths, but the detector can miss gear when lighting or camera angle changes. We also have a known issue where the spoken status can lag behind the latest frame, so the user may hear feedback for an earlier image.
submission.accomplishments: We are proud to have a working prototype that takes a camera image through detection and produces a spoken response. Building around a small vision model let us explore the whole interaction in the time available.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a vision result needs clear limits and context before it becomes useful guidance. Gemini helped us draft scenarios, while ElevenLabs made the feedback easier to follow without watching every status label.
submission.whats_next: We would improve the detector with more varied examples, make the voice feedback track the newest frame, and add a clear review step for a supervisor. We would also test the interface with event staff before considering real use.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used for organizing detection records but not in a central pipeline; the prototype works but has detection and feedback timing issues.

submission.name: Relief Gap Desk
submission.tagline: A clearer view of local needs and the resources assigned to them
submission.inspiration: Community relief groups can have many spreadsheets describing needs, donations, and active projects, but it is hard to see where coverage may be thin. We wanted to make those records easier for a local coordinator to scan and discuss.
submission.what_it_does: The dashboard maps sample community response areas and compares reported need with recorded support. It also flags unusual project-level ratios for review and has a Gemini panel intended to summarize what the data shows; a separate voice notification concept is still a stub.
submission.how_we_built_it: We prepared public and sample project data with Python, pandas, and SQL, then used Databricks to experiment with an Isolation Forest model for outlier detection. A Flask service and a simple JavaScript, HTML, and Tailwind map UI were built alongside it, but the model output and explanation panel are not yet fully connected.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the data shapes consistent across the notebook, service, and interface took longer than expected. We have working pieces for the map and model exploration, but a reliable deployed endpoint and verified Gemini summaries were not ready for the demo.
submission.accomplishments: We brought together a map concept, a data-preparation workflow, and an anomaly model experiment around a concrete coordination question. We also made a first pass at showing how an outlier might prompt a closer look rather than an automatic decision.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that an unusual ratio is only a lead for investigation; it does not explain why resources differ. Gemini helped us think through concise explanations, but those need to stay tied to the underlying records and sources.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the Databricks results to the dashboard, add source links and coordinator review notes, and test the workflow with a local relief organization. Forecasting and voice notifications would come later.

submission.name: CounterTalk
submission.tagline: Practice the English you need for a neighborhood shop shift
submission.inspiration: Some people learning English need to use it right away while handling everyday tasks at work. We wanted to make practice feel connected to situations like helping a customer or asking a coworker for clarification.
submission.what_it_does: Users choose a shop-floor situation and their comfort level, then get a short practice dialogue built around familiar vocabulary. The prototype also has a flashcard view and an audio playback path for hearing example phrases, though account onboarding and personalized vocabulary do not yet work as one flow.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Astro and React with Tailwind and Shadcn for the web interface, with a Go backend and Firebase for storing user data. Gemini generates draft dialogues and ElevenLabs can read sample lines aloud; the app pieces are present, but the complete account-to-practice path failed during the demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The biggest issue was connecting onboarding vocabulary to the generated exercises and saved progress. We also hit Gemini API limits while iterating, and our Go service was new to several of us, so some endpoints remained disconnected from the screens.
submission.accomplishments: We made several screens for choosing a situation, reviewing words, and practicing sample lines. We are proud that teammates learned unfamiliar tools while still producing something we could click through.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that personalization depends on getting a small amount of user information reliably through the whole app. Gemini helped us create dialogue drafts, and ElevenLabs showed how audio can support practice, but both need tighter integration with the learner's chosen level.
submission.whats_next: We would fix the account and vocabulary flow, make generated dialogues easier to review for naturalness, and add a more dependable audio playback experience. We would also ask language learners which work situations are most useful to practice.

challenge_results.rationale: The app improves language learning for work contexts but lacks direct financial services integration.

submission.name: Farewise
submission.tagline: Understand the small travel costs that shape a student trip.
submission.inspiration: As students moving between campus, home, and internships, we kept losing track of how fares, rideshares, and add-on fees accumulated. We wanted a tool that could explain those patterns in a practical way instead of leaving people with a pile of totals.
submission.what_it_does: Farewise groups sample transportation transactions into daily and category views, calling out fees, busy spending days, and rideshare versus transit use. Gemini turns those figures into short explanations, and a chat panel lets users ask basic questions about the displayed data.
submission.how_we_built_it: A FastAPI service normalizes transaction data from the Nessie API and calculates the core metrics, then exposes them to a Next.js and React interface written in TypeScript. We pass those summaries to Gemini for explanations; the demo works end to end, though some API data and chat responses can be inconsistent.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Keeping the deterministic calculations separate from generated explanations took some iteration, especially when the model described a pattern the metrics did not support. We also had trouble with occasional Nessie data gaps, so the dashboard can show incomplete travel activity.
submission.accomplishments: We connected transaction ingestion, calculated summaries, generated explanations, and a basic chat experience in one demo. We are proud the financial education angle stays grounded in visible numbers rather than asking Gemini to do the calculations.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to give an AI model structured summaries instead of raw transaction records and to check its output against the source figures. Building across the API and frontend also taught us to agree on data shapes early.
submission.whats_next: We would improve the data coverage and add clearer controls for correcting transaction categories. We would also make the explanations easier to review and give users a way to compare different trip plans.

challenge_results.rationale: Farewise addresses a meaningful student financial process by integrating transaction normalization, pattern detection, and AI explanations, though finance remains a secondary framing to the core data analysis.

submission.name: Tab Tally
submission.tagline: Make group takeout spending visible before it crowds out the rest of the budget.
submission.inspiration: Our friend group kept ordering food between classes and then wondering where the week’s spending had gone. We wanted a low-pressure way for campus club members to set a shared takeout limit and see how their habits were adding up.
submission.what_it_does: Tab Tally lets a small group log restaurant visits and compare its weekly takeout spending with a target. Members can enter a purchase manually or use a small Bluetooth button at a shared club table to prompt a visit entry. A Gemini helper can turn the group’s recent totals into a short budget suggestion, and an ElevenLabs voice reads the reminder aloud; Databricks is used for a basic weekly pattern summary.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built the mobile interface with React Native Expo and TypeScript, and Firebase stores group, visit, and spending records so members see the same totals. A low-cost Bluetooth button sends a visit prompt to the phone; the app then asks the member to confirm the place and amount, which keeps the hardware from recording purchases automatically. Firebase data is exported as a small table for a Databricks summary, while Gemini drafts a suggestion from the current group total and ElevenLabs speaks the reminder. The BNY connection is the shared spending workflow, with the app helping a group keep a simple budget visible.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the Bluetooth button to reconnect consistently was the main hardware issue, and a missed press means a visit needs to be added manually. Expo package setup and Android device pairing also took longer than we expected. The core entry and group total flow works, but notifications sometimes arrive late and the Databricks view only refreshes when we rerun the export.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a physical prompt to a shared mobile spending log and got a basic group view running end-to-end. We are proud that the button is optional: people can still log a meal when the phone or pairing is being difficult. The voice reminder makes a weekly total easier to notice without turning the app into a competition about individuals.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that even a simple hardware trigger adds pairing and battery problems that a screen-only prototype avoids. Firebase made it straightforward to share updates, while Databricks gave us a first look at summarizing group records outside the app. Gemini helped draft short reminder language, and ElevenLabs let us hear how that reminder would sound in use.
submission.whats_next: We would improve Bluetooth reconnection and add a clearer offline queue so entries are not lost when campus Wi-Fi drops. We also want the weekly summary to refresh automatically and let groups choose whether reminders are spoken, shown, or muted.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks provides a basic weekly pattern summary from Firebase data, but the core spending log works without it.
