submission.name: Lecture Bridge
submission.tagline: Listen to a class explanation in another language while keeping the original lecture in view.
submission.inspiration: International students in our group described how difficult it can be to follow a fast lecture while also trying to translate unfamiliar terms. We wanted to put translated audio and subtitles next to the browser video, so students could keep their attention on the class material.
submission.what_it_does: Lecture Bridge is a Chrome extension that captures a short audio chunk from a lecture tab, transcribes it, translates the text, and shows subtitles with synthesized speech in the selected language. Deepgram handles transcription, DeepL handles translation, and ElevenLabs provides the spoken output. Gemini is used for an optional brief glossary explanation, while a small Databricks notebook is intended to organize language and usage samples; neither is required for the main translation flow. The financial-services connection is a secondary accessibility use case for listening to short banking help clips in another language.
submission.how_we_built_it: The extension popup lets the user choose a language and start or stop capture, while a background script coordinates audio chunks and API requests. An offscreen document plays the generated audio because the service worker cannot play it directly, and a content script places subtitles over the active page. We kept the Deepgram to DeepL to ElevenLabs sequence from our initial design and added Gemini only for a glossary action. The pieces were developed by separate teammates, and the extension currently has mocked responses in place of a completed end-to-end pipeline.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We did not connect all of the extension components by demo time. Audio capture, subtitle rendering, and speech playback each work in isolation, but messages between the background worker and offscreen page are not reliable, so a translated chunk can fail to appear or play. We also did not finish handling the timing difference between subtitles and generated speech, and the Databricks and Gemini additions remain prototypes.
submission.accomplishments: We built the popup, subtitle overlay, and audio playback pieces and established the intended API sequence. We are proud that the extension has a clear browser-based interaction and does not require students to move lecture content into a separate app. The parts give us a practical base for finishing the integration.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a Chrome extension has several separate execution contexts, and audio has to be passed carefully between them. ElevenLabs made the translated text usable as speech, while Gemini helped us explore concise glossary explanations. We also learned that a multi-service pipeline needs clear failure states when any API call stalls.
submission.whats_next: We would finish the message flow between capture, translation, subtitles, and playback, then test it on a small set of lecture videos. We also want to add retry handling and make the glossary and sample analysis optional features that do not interrupt the main audio experience.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is central to the audio interaction but the pipeline is incomplete with mocked responses and unreliable component communication.

submission.name: Campus Signal Desk
submission.tagline: Bring scattered campus incident reports into one map for a human team to review.
submission.inspiration: A campus disruption can generate reports in different places: a facilities note, a student message, or an emergency call. We wanted a shared screen that helps a campus response team see those reports together and decide what needs attention, without claiming that software should dispatch help on its own.
submission.what_it_does: Campus Signal Desk accepts sample incident reports from several sources, uses Gemini agents to extract locations and summarize what may be happening, and assigns a rough priority for human review. A map shows the reported locations and can display suggested routes between them and campus response points. Databricks is used to group sample reports by type and time, and ElevenLabs can read a short incident summary aloud for staff who are monitoring the map. The system does not connect to live emergency calls or send responders.
submission.how_we_built_it: The React and Leaflet frontend requests a run from a FastAPI backend and listens for server-sent events as sample reports are processed. Gemini handles language-based extraction and summaries, while ordinary backend code places incidents into a review list and requests route geometry from OSRM. We used a small Databricks analysis to explore how incident categories cluster across the sample set, with results shown as a simple supporting view. ElevenLabs reads selected summaries so an operator can hear the key details while keeping the map visible; we chose this flow to keep all routing and prioritization reviewable by people.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The demo does not work end-to-end yet. The report cards and Gemini summaries can be produced, and the map can render sample points, but the route objects sometimes fail to reach the frontend because their geometry payload is too large for the current event flow. We also have not connected the Databricks summary or voice playback to the live run, so those parts are separate demonstrations.
submission.accomplishments: We built the core report review screen and a backend path that can summarize sample incidents. The map gives the project a concrete shared view, and we are proud that the prototype keeps a person in control of any response decision. We also identified a specific integration issue with transporting detailed route data.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that language models are useful for turning reports into structured fields, but route calculation should stay in ordinary code and route geometry should not be pushed through a model response. Gemini helped us prototype report extraction and summaries, while building the map taught us to pay attention to payload size and event timing. We also saw how a shared review queue can make multiple data sources easier to compare.
submission.whats_next: We would move route geometry into a direct backend response or a stored run object, then connect it reliably to the map. We also want to link the voice and Databricks views to the same run and test the interface with more varied sample reports before considering any live data source.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used for clustering incident reports but is not central to the main user flow, which relies on Gemini and manual review; the system shows partial integration with some features working separately.

submission.name: TradeBridge
submission.tagline: Help Central Florida contractors find available skilled workers and show workers their next step.
submission.inspiration: Around Orlando, construction and facilities teams can lose time searching for people with the right trade skills. We wanted to make that process clearer for both sides, especially for workers moving between projects.
submission.what_it_does: Employers can paste a short-term trade job and get a list of potential matches with the relevant skills highlighted. Workers can view a suggested certification or training step, while employers can select several candidates for follow-up.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a React and TypeScript interface with a FastAPI backend, SQLAlchemy, and PostgreSQL. Gemini is used as a secondary helper to turn pasted job descriptions into structured requirements; the matching flow uses those requirements against sample worker profiles.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The job parsing and candidate matching pieces work separately, but we did not get every path connected reliably during the weekend. We also had to make guesses about how to represent experience and certifications, so match scores are only a rough guide.
submission.accomplishments: We put together a working job input screen, a small candidate view, and an early certification suggestion flow. We are proud that the prototype focuses on helping workers understand why a role might fit instead of only showing a score.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that trade experience is difficult to reduce to a few fields, and that a language model needs constrained output to make job requirements usable. Gemini helped us explore how to extract requirements, but we still needed to check its results against our own schema.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the employer and worker flows, improve how licenses and job sites are represented, and test the matching process with local contractors and trade workers. Automated license checks could come later once we know which regional sources are available.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini helps parse job descriptions into structured requirements for matching, but core flows are not fully connected and match scoring is approximate.

submission.name: Receipt Ledger
submission.tagline: Turn a small business receipt pile into a clearer cash flow picture.
submission.inspiration: Student-run market stalls and small vendors often have sales records in one place and purchase receipts somewhere else, making it hard to see what a week of trading actually cost. We combined transaction summaries with receipt scanning to give those records a shared starting point.
submission.what_it_does: Users can upload a receipt image and a CSV of sales or expenses to build a simple weekly view of money in and money out. Gemini extracts likely line items and suggests categories, while a small inventory list can be updated from purchased items; extraction sometimes misses quantities or merges lines.
submission.how_we_built_it: The prototype uses a React and TypeScript frontend with a Node and Express backend and MongoDB persistence. Gemini processes receipt images and CSV headers, while the inventory idea borrows a receipt-to-items flow; the upload view and summary view work, but the inventory update is not reliable for every receipt.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Receipts vary in layout and image quality, and Gemini occasionally produces incomplete item details that make inventory counts wrong. We also had limited time to reconcile receipts against sales, so the weekly totals should be treated as an organizer rather than formal bookkeeping.
submission.accomplishments: We connected receipt uploads and transaction files to a basic cash flow screen for a small vendor scenario. We are glad the prototype can turn several awkward inputs into a view that is easier to scan.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that AI extraction needs a clear review step before data affects totals or inventory. Combining document parsing with ordinary financial records also exposed how many assumptions a simple dashboard can hide.
submission.whats_next: We would add a correction flow for parsed items and improve reconciliation between purchases and sales. Longer term, we would make the export useful for a bookkeeper without presenting the prototype as accounting software.

challenge_results.rationale: The Receipt Ledger addresses a meaningful financial process improvement for small businesses by integrating receipt scanning and transaction summaries, though extraction limitations and partial inventory reliability affect functionality.

submission.name: PlayByPlay Pal
submission.tagline: A spoken, plain-language guide to following campus soccer highlights.
submission.inspiration: We wanted friends who are new to soccer to enjoy campus match clips without needing to know every rule or player. A short, friendly spoken explanation seemed like a way to make highlights easier to follow together.
submission.what_it_does: The demo lets a user choose a soccer highlight clip and request a simple explanation of the play, then generates a spoken version with ElevenLabs. Clip selection and text generation work in separate parts, so the narration is not consistently timed to the video yet.
submission.how_we_built_it: A React frontend handles clip selection and playback, an Express server passes requests to a small Python transcript and explanation service, and ElevenLabs generates audio from the resulting text. Gemini through OpenRouter is used for the plain-language explanation, though the services are still stitched together manually in the demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Coordinating video, transcript, explanation, and audio responses across several services made timing difficult. Some clips have no usable transcript, and in those cases the explanation or narration can be missing or generic.
submission.accomplishments: We got a basic path from a selected clip to an AI explanation and generated voice working. We are proud of the direction for making sports clips more welcoming to newcomers, even though the full playback experience needs more integration.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much audio latency affects a feature that is meant to accompany video, and how useful ElevenLabs can be for turning short text into listenable narration. Gemini helped us test different explanation styles, but transcript quality remains important.
submission.whats_next: We would connect clip transcripts and audio playback more reliably, then add a few explanation styles for different experience levels. We would also make it easier to use clips with captions or transcripts already available.

challenge_results.rationale: The submission describes a central ElevenLabs audio role in explaining soccer highlights, but functionality is limited by incomplete integration.

submission.name: Campus Detour
submission.tagline: Explore a campus route with data-informed points of attention and spoken context.
submission.inspiration: Visitors and students walking between unfamiliar parts of a large campus may want more context than a fastest-route line provides. We prototyped a route view that highlights places to pay attention to, using available incident data as one imperfect signal.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype maps a route between campus locations and can show nearby historical incident clusters as context. Gemini can summarize a cluster in plain language and ElevenLabs can read the summary aloud, but those parts are demoed separately and the route does not yet update dynamically from them.
submission.how_we_built_it: We prepared sample geospatial records in Databricks and used clustering to create areas that can be displayed on a map. A lightweight routing service connects to Here Routing, while separate Gemini and ElevenLabs calls generate optional text and audio summaries; the full pipeline is not yet reliably connected.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The incident records are incomplete and delayed, so clusters can give a misleading picture if treated as current safety information. We also ran into polyline handling issues and did not finish wiring data updates through the map and narration flow.
submission.accomplishments: We explored a Databricks workflow for turning location records into map-ready clusters and paired that with a route prototype. We also demonstrated how a short text explanation could be generated and spoken for a location on the map.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much cleanup geospatial data needs before a cluster is useful, and that historical incidents cannot stand in for real-time conditions. Trying Gemini and ElevenLabs showed us how summaries and audio could make dense map data easier to approach.
submission.whats_next: We would improve the data freshness and source labeling, then connect cluster selection to the route and spoken summary. We would also add clearer map context so people can interpret the data carefully.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides optional audio summaries of incident clusters in a campus route prototype, which is a meaningful secondary feature but not central to the main flow.

submission.name: LabPath
submission.tagline: Turn a training goal into a short course plan for your next lab skill.
submission.inspiration: Students often need to learn a specific tool or procedure before a project, but broad online courses can be hard to fit around a deadline. We wanted a way to turn a learner’s goal into a focused path with a few useful resources.
submission.what_it_does: Learners enter a skill goal and their current experience, then receive a sequence of short lessons and suggested videos. A Databricks notebook groups sample learning topics and activity data into skill areas, which the app uses to shape the course outline.
submission.how_we_built_it: The app uses Next.js and JavaScript with Gemini to draft course steps, and YouTube API results to attach relevant videos. We prepared a small learning dataset in Databricks and used its analysis to organize topic suggestions; Neon and Drizzle hold course records, with Firebase used for some user data.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The flow works end to end in the demo, but generated lessons sometimes repeat or point to videos that do not quite match the topic. Getting the Databricks output, Gemini course draft, and two different data stores to agree took more time than expected.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a learner prompt to a generated course outline and resource list, and got a small Databricks analysis to influence the suggested topics. The prototype gave us a useful starting point for skill-focused learning rather than a general course catalog.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a course generator needs good topic data as well as a capable model, and that data preparation affects what the learner sees. Gemini helped draft explanations, while Databricks helped us see how to group the learning topics into a more usable path.
submission.whats_next: We would improve the topic dataset, add simple progress tracking, and check video relevance before showing recommendations. We also want to make the generated sequence easier to edit when a learner already knows part of a skill.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used to group learning topics and influence course outlines, but integration is limited and results are not fully utilized in the main flow.

submission.name: ReviewMap
submission.tagline: Give your lab team a shared map of the sources behind a research question.
submission.inspiration: When students split a research topic across a project team, it is easy to miss how their sources relate or which themes have little coverage. We wanted to help campus research groups organize reading before they prepare a proposal.
submission.what_it_does: A team can add paper links or DOIs, view citation connections, and ask Gemini questions grounded in the papers that were ingested. Databricks is used to group paper topics and surface areas with relatively few sources; a short ElevenLabs audio summary is an optional way to review a finding.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a React and Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL with pgvector, and background jobs for paper ingestion. Semantic Scholar supplies metadata, Gemini handles grounded questions and topic labels, and a Databricks notebook explores the source collection; ElevenLabs is used for a brief spoken recap.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The paper lookup and graph view ran as separate pieces, but our full ingestion-to-gap-to-chat demo failed when jobs did not finish consistently. Some imported papers had sparse metadata, which also made the topic groups and spoken recap less useful.
submission.accomplishments: We built an initial citation graph view and got individual paper lookup and Gemini question answering working on a small collection. The Databricks analysis gave us a first way to inspect topic coverage, and we added an audio recap as a small accessibility option.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that research tools depend on dependable source metadata and clear definitions of what counts as a gap. Gemini was helpful for summarizing and labeling, but it could not compensate for missing papers or broken ingestion steps.

submission.name: SunSafe Scout
submission.tagline: A campus skin check companion that helps you track a spot and decide what to ask a clinician.
submission.inspiration: Students spend long days outdoors around campus and may not know when a changing spot is worth asking about. We built a simple way to record what someone noticed and provide calm, general information to help them prepare a question for a clinician.
submission.what_it_does: The app guides a user through a skin spot questionnaire and photo capture, then combines those details with an image model result to produce a plain-language summary and suggested next steps. Gemini helps phrase the result, and an ElevenLabs voice option can read the guidance aloud.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React Native with Expo and TypeScript, a Hugging Face image classifier, and Gemini to combine the questionnaire with the classifier output. ElevenLabs provides spoken playback for the summary; the app keeps the flow focused on informational guidance rather than diagnosis.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting consistent photos across different lighting and camera conditions was difficult, and we had to keep the generated wording measured. The prototype runs through the capture and summary flow, but its output is not medically validated.
submission.accomplishments: We connected guided photo capture, a questionnaire, image classification, and a readable result in one mobile flow. We also made the same summary available as audio for users who prefer to listen.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that model output needs careful context and plain language, especially when people may be worried about what they see. Gemini helped us turn structured inputs into a summary, while the voice feature showed how delivery can affect the experience.
submission.whats_next: We would add a history view for comparing a person’s own observations over time and seek clinical review before expanding the guidance. Improving image quality checks and accessibility would also be priorities.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides optional spoken playback for a skin check summary, making it a meaningful secondary audio feature that supports accessibility but isn't central to the app's core functionality.

submission.name: Crew Kitchen
submission.tagline: Help student club treasurers plan shared meals from the food already in their kitchen.
submission.inspiration: Student groups often buy food for meetings while ingredients from an earlier event sit unused. We wanted a mobile-friendly way for a club to track what it has and turn that list into a meal plan with a rough spending view.
submission.what_it_does: A user can scan ingredients, keep a shared kitchen list, and ask Gemini for meal ideas based on what is available. The prototype also sketches a per-meeting cost estimate so a treasurer can compare a plan with the group’s budget.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Expo, React Native, and TypeScript for the app, with FastAPI, Firebase Auth, and Firestore behind it. Google Cloud Vision handles ingredient detection and Gemini suggests recipes; the budget view is a lightweight calculation over entered prices.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The scan and recipe screens worked independently, but the full flow from a photo into a saved shared inventory failed during our demo. Firebase state also did not consistently refresh across devices, so the budget view could be based on an incomplete list.
submission.accomplishments: We built the main mobile screens for scanning, inventory, and meal suggestions, and connected Gemini to a sample ingredient list. The budget estimate gave us a small way to adapt the cooking idea for student organizations.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that shared inventory needs reliable syncing before recipe suggestions feel trustworthy. Gemini could suggest practical combinations, but the usefulness still depended on accurate ingredient data and prices.
submission.whats_next: We would fix photo-to-inventory persistence, add clearer quantity and expiration fields, and let club members agree on a meal plan before shopping. We would also refine the cost estimate with locally entered prices.

challenge_results.rationale: The app addresses a specific financial workflow for student clubs by integrating inventory tracking and budgeting, but the core functionality has limitations and incomplete integration.

submission.name: RideKind
submission.tagline: Find a shared ride that fits your route and your footprint.
submission.inspiration: Long trips to campus events and weekend meetups can be expensive when everyone drives alone. We wanted a simple way for students heading in similar directions to find each other and make carpooling feel practical.
submission.what_it_does: RideKind lets a driver post a trip and lets riders look for trips by destination, timing, and vehicle type. It shows possible matches with a rough emissions comparison to help people consider sharing the ride.
submission.how_we_built_it: We sketched the trip and match screens in Figma, then built a React interface for searching and posting rides. A small Python backend stores trip details and handles matching; we planned to use Databricks to prepare trip and distance data for the emissions view, but that part did not connect to the full demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We lost time settling on the project, which left less time for wiring the pieces together. The ride screens and backend routes run in isolation, but posting a trip through to a complete match did not work reliably, and our analytics view stayed unfinished.
submission.accomplishments: We made a usable set of ride search and posting screens and got the basic backend pieces running. We also defined a first pass at matching around route, timing, and vehicle details.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that even a simple matching feature depends on consistent trip data and clear assumptions about what counts as a useful match. Working with Databricks also showed us that analytics needs a prepared dataset and a working path back to the interface.
submission.whats_next: We would connect trip creation, search, and match results into one dependable flow. Then we would finish the Databricks emissions summary and add clearer pickup coordination.

challenge_results.rationale: The project shows a meaningful data preparation step in Databricks but it is not yet connected to the main product flow.

submission.name: SpendSidetalk
submission.tagline: See your spending, then ask what the numbers mean.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make a bank statement less like a wall of transactions and more like a useful conversation. A chart can show where money went, while a plain-language assistant can help someone make sense of the pattern.
submission.what_it_does: Users can upload a transaction CSV and view spending grouped into categories with a basic chart. A chat panel is designed for questions about those totals, and a read-aloud control can speak a response for people who prefer listening. We also borrowed the idea of showing deposits and withdrawals alongside purchases, so the overview includes money coming in as well as going out.
submission.how_we_built_it: The browser interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for file upload, the spending chart, and audio controls. A Flask service in Python parses the CSV and exposes transaction summaries to the chat flow, which was prototyped with Gemini; ElevenLabs generates spoken versions of assistant replies. Databricks was an optional experiment for grouping transactions, but it is not part of the connected demo. The upload, chat, and audio pieces can each be shown, though their data handoff is incomplete, so the displayed conversation does not consistently reflect the uploaded file.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: CSV files vary in column names, date formats, and how they represent deposits, so the parser needs more cleanup than we expected. The frontend, Flask routes, model calls, and audio playback were built as separate pieces, and we ran out of time before connecting them into a reliable single flow. That means the chat can fall back to sample context instead of the current upload.
submission.accomplishments: We got a transaction upload view, a category breakdown, and separate chat and speech prototypes working. We are proud that the interface gives users a visual summary and a spoken option, even though the full connection still needs work.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a helpful answer depends on clean data and passing the right summary through every layer of the app. Gemini helped us draft conversational responses, while ElevenLabs let us explore spoken output; both still need careful integration to stay grounded in a user's own transactions.
submission.whats_next: We would standardize more CSV formats and connect each uploaded file to its chart and chat context. We would also finish the Databricks experiment as a repeatable transaction analysis step and improve the audio controls for longer replies.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is mentioned as an optional experiment not part of the connected demo, with incomplete data handoff between components limiting functionality and relevance.

submission.name: PitchQuest
submission.tagline: Practice interview answers in the way that works for you.
submission.inspiration: Interview practice often assumes everyone wants to type answers in English. We wanted a small practice room where students could prepare from their own experience and try voice or basic signing input.
submission.what_it_does: Upload a resume to get a few tailored practice questions, then answer by speaking in English or Spanish, typing, or trying letter-by-letter ASL input. The app asks a follow-up based on the answer and can read prompts aloud. Resume parsing and ASL recognition are rough, and ASL input is limited to fingerspelling rather than full sign language.
submission.how_we_built_it: A React interface sends resume text and answers to a FastAPI backend in Python. The backend uses resume sections to prompt question generation and follow-ups, while ElevenLabs speaks the questions and Gemini helps rephrase an answer into a short practice tip. MediaPipe extracts hand landmarks for a small scikit-learn classifier that attempts letter recognition; that path runs but sometimes confuses letters in changing light.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The ASL letter recognizer is unreliable when hands move quickly or lighting changes. We also saw intermittent failures in the speech browser API, so a voice answer can stop before the user is done.
submission.accomplishments: We connected resume-based questions, spoken prompts, and answer capture into a practice loop that works most of the time. It was satisfying to get several input modes into one demo, even with the signing path still limited.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that adding an input mode means designing feedback for it, not just connecting a model. Gemini helped us shape question and coaching text, while testing ElevenLabs made us pay attention to how voice timing affects a practice session.
submission.whats_next: We would improve the ASL input beyond isolated letters and make speech capture more dependable. We would also save sessions so users could revisit their answers and choose which practice mode to use by default.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs is central to the main user flow by speaking questions, but the ASL input and speech capture have reliability issues.

submission.name: WireWatch
submission.tagline: Catch suspicious payment requests before they reach the next step.
submission.inspiration: Small business finance teams can receive convincing emails asking them to change payment details or rush a transfer. We wanted to give staff a quick way to review those messages before acting.
submission.what_it_does: Paste a payment-related email into WireWatch to get a Gemini-generated review of suspicious wording, sender claims, and link text. The result can be read aloud with ElevenLabs so a reviewer can hear the main warning signs while checking the message.
submission.how_we_built_it: We kept a lightweight HTML, CSS, and JavaScript page with a Python service for the analysis request. Gemini handles the message review, and ElevenLabs turns the explanation into audio; the email input and response panels work, but the API connection is mocked in the current demo, so analysis and playback do not reliably follow the submitted text.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Connecting the model response to the interface took longer than expected, and the demo still uses placeholder results in places. We also need better handling for email headers and links before this could fit into a real financial workflow.
submission.accomplishments: We built the review screen and explored a way to explain payment-email warning signs in plain language. The prototype gave us a clear starting point for a focused financial services tool.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to keep API keys out of browser code and to treat model output as a review aid rather than a final decision. Gemini helped draft contextual explanations, and ElevenLabs gave those explanations a spoken form.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the backend analysis and speech calls end to end, then add a way for finance staff to mark a message for human follow-up. We would also test the review against more varied payment request examples.

challenge_results.rationale: WireWatch addresses a meaningful financial workflow problem with a plausible technical approach but lacks full implementation evidence.

submission.name: TrailBite
submission.tagline: Make a lighter pack from the food you already have.
submission.inspiration: Students planning a day hike or overnight trip often buy new snacks because it is hard to tell what can travel well from the kitchen. We wanted to help people turn familiar ingredients into a simple trail meal plan.
submission.what_it_does: Take or choose a photo of food and get a rough list of likely ingredients, then ask for a compact meal or snack idea suited to a short trip. The app has a small inventory screen and can read a suggested recipe aloud, but the mobile scan-to-recipe flow did not work end to end in our demo.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Expo with React Native and TypeScript for the mobile screens, plus a FastAPI backend in Python. Gemini generates trail-friendly meal suggestions, Google Cloud Vision was used for a separate ingredient scan experiment, and ElevenLabs can speak a recipe response. The inventory screen and AI calls run as separate parts, but scan results do not reliably reach the recipe prompt yet.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting camera permissions and image results through the mobile app took longer than expected. We did not finish connecting the scan output to the inventory and recipe request, so the demo needs manual ingredient entry for the useful part.
submission.accomplishments: We made the meal suggestion and spoken recipe pieces work independently and built the mobile screens around a clear trip-planning use. We learned what needs to connect before a photo can actually save someone time.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that vision output is only useful when it reaches the next step in the product. Gemini helped generate practical meal ideas, and ElevenLabs made them easier to follow hands-free.
submission.whats_next: We would connect camera detection, saved ingredients, and recipe suggestions into one flow. We would also add simple packing and storage notes for common day-trip foods.

submission.name: Deadline Reef
submission.tagline: Turn school tasks into a small game where your sea buddy perks up when you stay on schedule.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make keeping up with community center activities feel less like another checklist for kids. A little companion and a few rewards seemed like a friendly way to help young members remember their projects and show up for group activities.
submission.what_it_does: Kids add activities and due dates to a sidebar, then earn coins when they mark work complete. A sea creature’s mood changes based on how close to the deadline they finish, and the small shop lets them spend coins on another pet or accessories. The app is aimed at youth programs rather than a school assignment system.
submission.how_we_built_it: The sidebar uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with a FastAPI service written in Python behind it. The browser sends task updates to the service, which keeps the current task and coin data in JSON so the interface can refresh. We made the artwork ourselves in Aseprite.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting two interface pieces built with different assumptions to work together took time. The main task flow runs through the API, but the data is only stored in JSON and can be unreliable; a restart or an unexpected update can leave progress out of sync. We had to leave the shop and progression system fairly small.
submission.accomplishments: We made original pet and interface art and connected task completion to the creature’s mood and coin balance. The core loop works from adding a task through marking it done and seeing the reward appear.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a quick prototype still benefits from deciding early where each piece of state lives. AI coding help was useful for getting unstuck on small implementation questions, but we still had to check how the browser and API handled updates together.
submission.whats_next: We would like to make task and reward data persist more safely, then add more creatures and items. A next version could also let a youth group share activities and see each other’s pets, with clear privacy controls.

challenge_results.rationale: The project combines a game-like interface with task management for youth programs, showing originality but not uniqueness.

submission.name: Vault Showdown
submission.tagline: Settle a casino dispute in a two-player card duel controlled by a chunky handheld.
submission.inspiration: We like quick card games where a round can turn on one bold move, and wanted to make the players physically act out their choices. We shifted the setting to a small financial office simulation: two staff members compete to uncover a suspicious cash discrepancy before the vault closes.
submission.what_it_does: Two players face off in a short card duel, using a thick card-shaped controller to trigger actions that appear in the game. The round is framed around checking transactions and spotting the discrepancy, with a score deciding who resolves the case. It is a game scenario, not a real financial monitoring tool.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made the game in Godot and used a Raspberry Pi Pico controller to send button and movement data to a Python process over serial. Python converts that input into messages sent to Godot over UDP, where the game applies the actions to the current round. We used GitHub for version control and added a simple mock transaction ledger as the duel’s financial context.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Serial values needed to be parsed and translated consistently before Godot could use them, and the hardware drivers added another point of failure. Animation and engine issues also slowed us down, while merging Godot project changes sometimes introduced dependency problems. submission.name: Closet Callboard
submission.tagline: Plan practical outfits for campus gigs from the clothes you already have.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to help students who have to move between class, a club event, and a part-time shift without changing outfits. Picking something comfortable for Florida weather while still fitting the occasion can take longer than it should.
submission.what_it_does: Users can photograph clothes and ask for outfit ideas for a campus event or work shift, with local weather as a small input. The app is meant to suggest combinations from the saved wardrobe, but the full path from photo to recommendation did not come together reliably.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used React Native and Expo for a mobile prototype, with Gemini intended to identify clothing details from photos and help assemble suggestions. Weather data was meant to add a comfort hint, while local storage holds wardrobe entries on the phone. We also tried a small Databricks notebook to summarize sample clothing categories, but it is separate from the working app flow.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The image upload, Gemini response, and saved wardrobe state did not stay connected consistently, so the demo only shows isolated pieces rather than a reliable end-to-end outfit recommendation. Databricks was an experiment with sample data and does not yet affect what the app displays.
submission.accomplishments: We built a mobile wardrobe screen and got parts of the photo and clothing-label flow running. The prototype gave us a concrete starting point for testing how wardrobe information could be organized on a phone.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that image compression, API response formats, and mobile storage all need to be planned together. We also got a first look at preparing simple category data in Databricks, though our notebook still needs a real connection to the app.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the photo labeling, wardrobe storage, weather lookup, and recommendation screen into one dependable flow. We would also make the Databricks analysis useful to the app, for example by showing what clothing categories are underrepresented in a sample wardrobe.

submission.name: Civic Call Desk
submission.tagline: Turn incoming city service calls into clearer handoffs and a live view of recurring neighborhood issues.
submission.inspiration: We were interested in the way a resident may have to explain a broken streetlight or missed pickup several times before it reaches the right department. The same handoff friction we noticed in healthcare can affect local services, especially when a busy desk is sorting calls and messages.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype takes a service-call transcript, creates a short summary with Gemini, and shows the status and key details on an operator dashboard. It groups sample issue reports by location and time so staff can notice a cluster, such as repeated water or road complaints. The dashboard updates live, but it is a workflow demo and does not dispatch city crews.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a web dashboard with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Recharts, backed by a small event-driven call store. Incoming call events are reconciled by the backend, then Gemini turns transcript text into structured issue fields and a summary; server-sent events carry updates to the dashboard. We prepared sample reports in Databricks and use its aggregation to power the neighborhood issue view, linking the resulting counts back to the operator screen.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Events can arrive out of order, and a live transcript update can trigger a stale summary if it races with another update. The dashboard sometimes needs a refresh to recover after that sequence. Our Databricks view depends on prepared sample data, so it is not yet a dependable signal for real service demand.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a transcript summary, live operator view, and location-based issue aggregation in one web demo. We are proud that an operator can follow a report from its incoming details to a broader pattern without leaving the dashboard.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to treat event ordering and state reconciliation as core product work in a real-time interface. Gemini helped structure informal reports, while Databricks made it easier to group prepared records; both still need clear validation before staff could rely on the output.
submission.whats_next: We would test with a larger, realistic set of anonymized service reports and make the event recovery behavior more robust. We would also add a human review step before any issue summary or cluster is routed to a department.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used for aggregation in the neighborhood issue view, which is part of the main product flow but not a central pipeline.

submission.name: Runway Reserve
submission.tagline: Play through a small business’s early money choices and see how steady investing changes the runway.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make investing feel less abstract for students who are starting a small side business or freelance gig. Those owners often have to decide what to keep as a cash buffer and what might be invested for later, while juggling unpredictable expenses.
submission.what_it_does: Players guide a fictional one-person business through monthly events, choosing how much income to hold as savings and how much to invest in a simulated index fund. The game compares the business’s cash runway and long-term balance across choices, with no real money involved. Short spoken explanations add context to key decisions, though the voice playback can occasionally fail.
submission.how_we_built_it: The web game uses React, Vite, and Tailwind for the screens, with MongoDB storing a player’s scenario progress. Node.js handles the game state and asks Gemini for occasional scenario text and plain-language explanations; core balances are calculated in the app so the model does not set the numbers. ElevenLabs turns selected explanations into audio, which the browser plays alongside each event. These parts connect through the Node API, but the audio request is the least reliable link.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Scoping the business scenarios and keeping the balance calculations consistent took more time than expected. The ElevenLabs response sometimes arrives after the player has moved to the next event, and generated scenario text can need editing to fit the game’s numbers. We have a playable path, but the spoken layer is not dependable every time.
submission.accomplishments: We built a complete short simulation where choices affect a business’s cash cushion and projected future balance. We are proud of having a concrete game loop and adding voice to some of the financial explanations.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to keep financial calculations deterministic even when AI helps write the surrounding explanation. React state and API timing also mattered more than we expected: the game has to know which event an audio response belongs to. Gemini and ElevenLabs were useful creative tools, but their outputs still needed guardrails and checks.
submission.whats_next: We would add more business events and let players compare different cash-buffer rules across a longer timeline. We also want to improve audio loading and let a player replay or skip narration without interrupting the scenario.

challenge_results.rationale: ElevenLabs provides central voice explanations for financial decisions in a business simulation game, though audio reliability issues affect functionality.

submission.name: SafeStep
submission.tagline: A camera checkpoint that helps makerspaces catch missing protective gear before a job starts.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make PPE checks easier in shared fabrication rooms where students move between tasks and supervisors cannot watch every entrance. A quick visual check felt more practical than relying on everyone to remember the full gear list each time.
submission.what_it_does: A member scans an RFID badge or enters a PIN, then stands at the checkpoint camera. The prototype checks for required gear and shows what it thinks is missing; staff can review recent entries and basic compliance trends in a dashboard. It also reads a short spoken reminder when someone needs to add equipment.
submission.how_we_built_it: A React and TypeScript dashboard talks to a Node.js server that stores profiles, room rules, and check-in logs in MongoDB. A local Flask service uses OpenCV and a YOLO model to inspect camera frames, while Gemini turns detected items into a plain-language prompt. We added ElevenLabs speech for that reminder and a small BNY-oriented view of check-in records as a workflow example for organizations managing risk.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting the camera service, server, and live dashboard to agree on each scan took time, and detection was inconsistent with poor lighting or gear partly out of frame. The end-to-end flow works in our demo, but the model can miss items and the records are not a substitute for an actual safety inspection.
submission.accomplishments: We connected badge and PIN input to a camera check and a saved entry log. We are proud that the prototype can give a specific spoken reminder instead of only showing a generic pass or fail.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how much coordination a small real-time system needs across Python vision code, a Node server, and a React screen. Gemini helped us prototype explanations, and we learned to treat those explanations as interface text rather than proof that a detection is correct.
submission.whats_next: We would test the detector with more gear types and varied workshop lighting, then add a staff review flow for uncertain scans. A standalone kiosk and a more useful audit export would also make the concept easier to try in a real makerspace.

submission.name: ClubCashflow
submission.tagline: A shared mobile view of recurring costs and incoming funds for student project teams.
submission.inspiration: Student teams often have dues, reimbursements, and event costs spread across conversations and separate notes. We wanted a lightweight way for a club to see what money is expected and what still needs attention.
submission.what_it_does: The app lets a group record planned expenses and incoming contributions, then view a weekly summary and reminders. Members can add an item manually or attach it to a group, with simple categories to help a treasurer prepare a handoff.
submission.how_we_built_it: We started a React Native Expo app backed by Firebase for users, groups, and entries. A small Databricks notebook explores grouped transaction data and produces a summary view concept, but it is not connected to the mobile screens yet.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The project does not run end-to-end: our Android device setup and package issues kept the app from reliably reaching Firebase, and the analytics output is separate. The group screens and data pieces run in isolation, but we did not finish a dependable demo flow.
submission.accomplishments: We made early versions of the group ledger and weekly summary screens, and defined the basic records a treasurer would need. We also got a first pass at preparing group spending data for analysis.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how quickly mobile setup problems can consume a short build window, and got more familiar with Firebase data structure. We also saw that analytics only helps once the app consistently supplies it with usable records.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the mobile forms to the shared ledger, finish login and group permissions, and feed the same records into the Databricks summary. After that, we would try a clearer reimbursement and approval flow for club treasurers.

challenge_results.rationale: The app improves a student club financial process with shared tracking but lacks end-to-end functionality and deeper financial integration.

submission.name: HandPause
submission.tagline: A small desktop buddy that nudges makers to rest their hands between long build sessions.
submission.inspiration: People who spend hours modeling, coding, or editing can lose track of how long they have been repeating the same hand movements. We wanted a simple reminder that feels friendly and is easy to pause when someone is in the middle of something.
submission.what_it_does: The Python desktop prototype counts down from a user-set work interval and opens a short hand-stretch break when time is up. A small animated companion changes expression to get attention, and an ElevenLabs voice can read a brief prompt; users choose a stretch and break length themselves.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Tkinter for the windows and timer, Python and PIL for the images, and basic animation logic for the companion. A separate Databricks notebook sketches how anonymized session lengths could be summarized into break patterns, while the app stores no connected analytics yet.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The desktop timer and companion run, but our full reminder flow did not connect reliably and the voice prompt sometimes failed to load. We did not finish the Databricks connection or any automatic activity sensing, so the timer cannot tell whether the user is actually at the computer.
submission.accomplishments: We got the timer controls and draggable animated companion working as separate pieces. We also made a basic stretch selection screen, even though the transitions between parts still need work.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned to keep a desktop interface manageable with Tkinter and to animate small image states. Our AI tool helped us draft reminder wording, but we had to keep the prompts short so they fit the break screen.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the screens into one stable flow and make missed voice playback fall back to on-screen text. Later, session summaries could help users choose a less disruptive reminder schedule, and a sensor could detect when someone has stepped away.

challenge_results.rationale: The project uses ElevenLabs for voice prompts in a meaningful secondary role, but the integration is not central to the core timer functionality and has reliability issues.

submission.name: Relief Rhythm
submission.tagline: Explore local supply gaps and hear a short practice track for planning a response.
submission.inspiration: During a response, teams need to compare reported needs with available resources and make sense of a changing situation. We wanted to pair a simple data view with a way for volunteers to rehearse the terminology and decisions they may encounter.
submission.what_it_does: The site maps sample regions by a gap score comparing reported needs with listed aid, and a selected region opens its risk indicators and suggested logistics. A practice mode generates a short backing track and a set of response terms for a volunteer to improvise over, with Gemini offering a brief reflection on the submitted notes.
submission.how_we_built_it: We prepared sample aid and need records with Python and pandas, then used Databricks to calculate and display regional gap summaries that drive the map colors. The web interface connects selection state to a detail panel; Gemini drafts region-specific planning prompts, while the practice mode borrows the configurable track and feedback idea from a music learning tool. BNY is represented by a small resource-allocation view, and the track is a secondary workflow rather than a financial product.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Joining the map, data summaries, and practice mode took more coordination than expected, and a few map selections did not refresh the detail panel at first. The main path works with our sample dataset, but the aid figures and recommendations are not validated for real deployments.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a regional gap view to a detail panel and a lightweight practice flow. We are glad the Databricks calculations affect the map instead of sitting in a separate notebook, and that the demo can move from a data point to a planning prompt.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a useful index depends on clear assumptions about what its inputs mean, and that those assumptions need to be visible. We also found that map state and generated practice content need separate interfaces so a change in one does not unexpectedly reset the other.
submission.whats_next: We would use better sourced and regularly updated data, add uncertainty notes to the gap scores, and ask aid practitioners to review the planning prompts. The practice mode could later accept voice recordings and give feedback on clarity and terminology.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks is used for regional gap calculations affecting the map but lacks detailed data flow explanations and deeper integration with other components.

submission.name: Market Minute
submission.tagline: Swipe through money explainers, then see how a simple investing rule reacts to market signals.
submission.inspiration: Short financial videos are easy to find, but it can be hard to tell whether a clip explains a useful idea or just makes a bold claim. We wanted to connect bite-sized learning with a small, transparent way to explore how market signals can inform a rule.
submission.what_it_does: The web prototype shows short finance explainers and lets users mark clips as useful, then presents a paper-trading sandbox with a few adjustable rules and sample sentiment signals. A rough content check uses sentence similarity to flag clips that appear off topic, and an ElevenLabs voice can read a clip summary aloud.
submission.how_we_built_it: The React and TypeScript interface has separate feed and sandbox views, while a FastAPI backend provides placeholder clip records and rule inputs. We prototyped sentence-transformer checks in Python and a market-signal calculation inspired by a trading-rule project, but those pieces are not wired into the feed or each other. The BNY angle is the financial education and decision-support workflow, and voice narration is an optional accessibility feature.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The demo is not connected end-to-end: the feed, similarity check, paper-trading calculation, and voice playback work only as separate pieces or mocked screens. We did not complete user accounts, real market data, or a rewards system, so the displayed signals should not be treated as investment advice.
submission.accomplishments: We built a navigable feed mockup and separate working prototypes for content similarity and a simple rule calculation. We are proud that the sandbox makes its inputs visible instead of presenting a mysterious prediction.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that financial content review is more nuanced than matching a clip to a topic label, and that market rules need clear assumptions. AI tools helped us sketch summaries and interface copy, but we still need human review before trusting generated explanations.
submission.whats_next: We would connect clip transcripts to the review service, add sourced market data for paper trading, and make the voice playback part of the clip view. A later version could include progress tracking and verified educational material without tying learning rewards to speculative token mechanics.

challenge_results.rationale: The submission addresses financial education and decision support with a prototype that connects learning content to a simple investing rule, but core components remain disconnected or mocked.

submission.name: Worldseed Workshop
submission.tagline: Sketch a tiny world, then try to make it playable.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to give campus clubs and first-time game makers a way to turn a theme into a small playable scene. A lot of people have ideas for characters and places but get stuck before opening a full game engine. We focused on a guided editor where the art can start from a prompt and the level rules stay adjustable. The goal was a quick creative exercise, not a replacement for professional game tools.
submission.what_it_does: Users can request a few simple character or object sprites and arrange them in a 2D level. The editor has basic platforms, hazards, a goal, and movement settings such as gravity and speed. A play view lets users test the layout, and a configuration string is intended to let someone else reopen a level. Our Gemini connection is used only for image generation, so most of the project is still the editor and game loop.
submission.how_we_built_it: The interface uses React with Tailwind, while Phaser handles the game scene and player movement. An Express server routes image requests to a small Python script that calls Gemini through Google Cloud, then returns the generated image for the editor to use. Level settings live in the browser as configuration data and feed into Phaser when a scene starts. This keeps the game loop separate from the image request path, though those two paths did not come together reliably in our demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting generated images into the right sprite dimensions took more work than expected, and our crop step sometimes cut off the subject. Gemini image generation is a small part of the app, and prompt changes did not always give us consistent results. We also ran short on time wiring saved configurations into the play view. The editor and game scene run in isolation, but the complete flow from prompt to saved, playable level failed during the demo.
submission.accomplishments: We got a basic level editor and a Phaser play scene running, with controls for a few movement settings. We also connected an image request path to Gemini and tried the returned art as game sprites. We are proud that the pieces show how a prompt-based art step could fit into a simple maker tool, even though the full experience is unfinished.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that generated art needs a predictable size and transparent background to behave like a game asset. We also learned how much care it takes to pass image files and level settings between a React editor, a server, and a game scene. Gemini helped us explore visual directions quickly, but we still needed manual cropping and prompt adjustments. Several of us were new to connecting a full stack app with a game engine.
submission.whats_next: We would first fix the handoff from the editor to the playable scene and make configuration sharing reliable. After that, we would add a basic sprite cleanup step and let users upload their own art. A small gallery for sharing levels could come later if the editor becomes stable.

submission.name: Lot Loop
submission.tagline: Make the last open spot a little less stressful.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to turn the scramble for a spot at a busy student event into a quick arcade game. The setting is a made-up UCF concert lot, where drivers weave around cones and other cars while trying to reach an open space first. It keeps the familiar parking pressure but gives it a playful, short-session format.
submission.what_it_does: Players steer through a crowded lot and race toward open spaces while avoiding obstacles. We added a simple boost pickup so players can make a risky dash when the route opens up. The game runs from start to finish, though collisions sometimes behave oddly and can leave a car stuck against a barrier.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Unity and C# for the driving, collision rules, and game flow. Photoshop was used for the bright car and lot art, and GitHub helped us work on separate parts of the project. The boost pickup is a small change to the core parking race and gives players a choice between a safe route and a faster one.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Unity scenes and shared assets caused a few confusing Git conflicts early on. We also had trouble tuning the car handling so the game felt chaotic without becoming frustrating. The demo is playable, but collisions near the edge of the lot can still trap the player.
submission.accomplishments: We made a complete short game loop with a start, a parking race, and a finish condition. We are happy with how the colorful visuals make a stressful lot feel silly and approachable.
submission.what_we_learned: We got more practice with Unity physics, C# event handling, and collaborating through version control. We also learned that small changes to steering and collision settings can have a large effect on whether a game feels fair.
submission.whats_next: We would add a pause screen and sound controls, then make a few different event lots with new obstacles. We would also revisit collision handling and tune the boost so it helps without making the race trivial.

submission.name: Catalyst Scout
submission.tagline: Explore enzyme candidates for compounds used in student lab projects.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make enzyme sequence exploration a little more approachable for students working with small chemistry examples. Protein models can produce results that are difficult to connect back to a molecule, so we built a rough interface around that input and output. We adapted the idea toward teaching and early exploration rather than making medical claims.
submission.what_it_does: A user enters a compound as a SMILES string and gets a candidate amino acid sequence to inspect. The page also aims to show a basic predicted structure so users can see a rough shape alongside the sequence. Results are exploratory suggestions, not verified enzymes or treatment guidance.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Python with pandas and NumPy to prepare a small set of compound and sequence pairs, then connected a transformer-based model workflow to the web interface. Databricks is used to organize the sample data and run a first-pass analysis of which compound groups appear in the dataset. The UI sends a SMILES input to the backend, which returns a candidate sequence and a summary; a structure-view step is included as a separate service. The sequence path works for some inputs, but the structure step and data workflow do not always respond in time.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Finding clean paired examples and mapping molecule strings to model inputs took most of our effort. We had limited compute and could not train a reliable model from scratch during the weekend. The Databricks analysis uses a small dataset, and the structure display can fail or time out, so outputs are not consistent.
submission.accomplishments: We connected a basic compound input form to a sequence generation path and made a simple data view in Databricks. We are proud that the project gave our team a concrete way to explore how chemical and protein data might meet in a web tool.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned more about protein language models, SMILES, and the difficulty of assembling useful biological data. Using Databricks also showed us how data preparation and analysis can support an application, even when the model itself is still rough.
submission.whats_next: We would expand and validate the paired dataset, compare model outputs against known examples, and make the structure view more dependable. A next version should clearly communicate confidence and provenance for every candidate.

challenge_results.rationale: Databricks supports data preparation and analysis but is not central to the main user flow; the prototype shows partial working core with some limitations in consistency and dataset size.

submission.name: LoopLens
submission.tagline: Trace a failing Python run and find the next clue.
submission.inspiration: We built this for students practicing small coding exercises who get stuck when a test fails. Seeing variables change can be more useful than rereading the same lines, so we tried to make a browser tool that turns a run into a visual trace.
submission.what_it_does: Users can enter Python and run it against a few sample cases, then view a basic step trace of variables and output. Gemini is meant to offer a short hint based on the error and trace. The editor and trace prototype run separately, and we did not get the complete run-to-hint flow working in the demo.
submission.how_we_built_it: The web app uses TypeScript and a Monaco-style editor, with Pyodide and WebAssembly intended to execute code in the browser. We extract output and error details for the trace view, then pass that context to Gemini for a nudge rather than a full solution. During the hackathon, the editor and Gemini request path were built, but the execution data did not reliably reach both the visualizer and hint prompt.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting consistent execution details out of browser-based Python was the main blocker. Our problem data also needed cleanup, and time ran out before the editor, runner, trace, and hint pieces were integrated end to end.
submission.accomplishments: We built a usable editor screen and separate prototypes for tracing output and requesting a Gemini hint. We are glad we found a direction for turning test failures into concrete visual clues.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how Pyodide and WebAssembly can run code in a browser, and how important a stable trace format is before asking Gemini for useful help.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the execution pipeline first, then improve the trace for loops and nested data. We would also add more practice problems and test whether hints remain grounded in actual runtime information.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini provides optional hints based on trace data, which is a meaningful secondary feature but not central to the core tracing functionality.

submission.name: Civic Beacon
submission.tagline: A shared incident map for neighborhood cleanup and recovery crews.
submission.inspiration: After seeing how storms can leave neighborhoods with scattered needs, we wanted a simple way for local volunteers and coordinators to share what is happening block by block. We focused on the period after the immediate emergency, when residents still need help and teams need a clearer picture.
submission.what_it_does: Residents can send a chat report about a blocked road, supply need, or other issue, which appears as a location on a shared map. Coordinators can review clusters of reports, ask Gemini questions about an area, and send updates to people nearby; the map also shows volunteer teams. We added a short spoken briefing for coordinators as a small voice feature.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used FastAPI for REST endpoints and a WebSocket for live updates, with PostgreSQL storing reports and their locations. A Gemini-backed retrieval flow is intended to answer questions using reports from a selected area, and React with Vite provides the resident and coordinator screens. We also tried Databricks to summarize report trends and included a BNY-themed resource status panel for tracking recovery supplies; the pieces are prototypes and are not fully connected.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Tuning report retrieval took longer than expected, and map layers were fiddly to line up. Our Gemini questions, Databricks summaries, voice briefing, and supply panel each have a basic path, but several do not yet share live data end to end.
submission.accomplishments: We got the core report and map experience running and connected it to a first pass at location-based questions. We are glad the prototype makes it possible to see incoming needs and coordinator updates in one place.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a retrieval system has to fit into the screens and data flow people actually use; building embeddings alone does not make answers useful. Gemini helped us shape and test the question flow, and we learned to check its responses against the reports behind them.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the analytics and voice briefing to the same live report stream, then test the map with local recovery coordinators. We also want clearer accessibility options and a way to mark reports resolved.

submission.name: LabLink Remote
submission.tagline: Let a teammate see your setup and help with the clicks.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make it easier for students to get hands-on help with a coding environment or a campus lab workstation. A call can show the problem, but it is often hard to point out the exact control or reproduce a sequence of steps together.
submission.what_it_does: A host shares a live view of their screen with a helper on the same local network. The helper can click or type into the shared view while the host can still use their own mouse and keyboard. Gemini has a small optional role suggesting a concise troubleshooting checklist from a typed description of the issue.
submission.how_we_built_it: The desktop client is built with Python and PySide6, using MSS to capture screen frames and OpenCV and Pillow for image handling. PyAutoGUI applies remote pointer and keyboard events, while a lightweight network connection sends frames and input between machines on the same Wi-Fi. We used Gemini to draft and refine the optional checklist prompt, but the screen sharing works independently of it.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Keeping the stream responsive while forwarding input was the main challenge. AI-generated code needed trimming and review, and the checklist is not tied to live screen contents, so it can miss details that a person can see.
submission.accomplishments: We connected screen viewing and remote input in a working local-network prototype. We are proud that the host can keep interacting while a helper demonstrates a step.
submission.what_we_learned: We got practice with screen capture, desktop UI events, and the tradeoffs between image quality and responsiveness. Gemini helped us get an initial checklist flow in place, but we still had to test the networking and input behavior ourselves.
submission.whats_next: We would work on lower-latency streaming, secure connections beyond the local network, and a clearer permission flow for remote input. Audio chat and profiles could also make longer help sessions easier.

challenge_results.rationale: Gemini's optional checklist role is minor and swappable, with screen sharing working independently.

submission.name: RouteReady Closet
submission.tagline: Choose a comfortable outfit for the route and weather ahead.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make getting dressed less of a daily puzzle, especially when a campus day includes a long walk between classes and changing weather. The idea was to use clothing photos to build a small wardrobe catalog, then bring route conditions into the choice.
submission.what_it_does: Users photograph clothes and Gemini extracts basic details such as color and garment type to make a digital closet. The app can suggest an outfit for the day using local weather and a selected destination, with a simple map view that highlights a route and reported trouble spots. Suggestions are limited to items in the saved closet, though the route information is a lightweight prototype.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a React Native and Expo app that stores compressed clothing images and item details on the device. Gemini analyzes an image and returns structured clothing metadata, while a weather service provides conditions for outfit suggestions. A map screen combines destination routing with a small set of safety notes inspired by public incident information; the route view and wardrobe advice are separate flows in this version.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Getting consistent clothing labels from varied photos took prompt adjustments, and image compression had to balance storage space with enough detail for recognition. The route feature is limited to a demo data set, so it cannot reliably represent current conditions or incidents.
submission.accomplishments: We built a usable flow from photographing a garment to seeing it in a closet and getting an outfit suggestion. We also connected that flow with a basic route screen so the app considers the shape of a campus day.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to request structured JSON from a vision model and handle on-device image storage in a mobile app. We also saw that maps and AI advice need clear data boundaries, since a polished suggestion can otherwise sound more certain than its inputs allow.
submission.whats_next: We would connect to dependable route and public safety data, and make the map notes easier to verify. We also want outfit planning for multiple stops and better controls for comfort preferences.

challenge_results.rationale: The app integrates weather and route data with a digital closet but has a limited prototype route feature and separate flows.

submission.name: Cashflow Canopy
submission.tagline: See how a small business’s transactions branch into everyday spending patterns.
submission.inspiration: We liked the idea of viewing information as connected pieces rather than rows in a spreadsheet. We wanted to apply that approach to a small shop’s transactions, where seeing how purchases relate to broader expense groups could help an owner decide what to review.
submission.what_it_does: The prototype imports sample transaction data from a CSV and displays purchases as nodes grouped under category nodes, sized by amount. A short AI-generated note calls out patterns in the sample data, such as a category that has grown between periods. Bank connections and live updates are not implemented.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used a TypeScript web interface with D3.js to render the transaction graph, plus a small Go service to parse CSV data into JSON. A Python script sends summarized data to Gemini for draft observations. The graph and analysis can be demonstrated separately, but their data handoff is still basic and some displayed insights use prepared examples.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We changed backend direction during the weekend and had to reshape the data flow while the graph was already underway. The category layout and AI analysis are both prototypes, and we have not connected them to actual banking data or validated the insights with business owners.
submission.accomplishments: We made a CSV-to-graph demo that lets viewers inspect spending by category and transaction. We are proud that the visual approach is clear enough to discuss, even while the analysis connection needs more work.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a financial visualization needs a useful question behind it, not just an interesting layout. Gemini can help draft observations from summarized data, but careful inputs and checks are needed before those notes could guide real decisions.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the import, graph, and analysis steps reliably, add controls for comparing date ranges, and test the tool with small business bookkeeping workflows. Secure account connections would be a later step.

challenge_results.rationale: The submission improves financial data visualization for small businesses but lacks implementation details and integration between components.
