submission.name: Break Bloom
submission.tagline: A small desktop garden that turns screen breaks into a routine you can shape.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make short breaks feel approachable for people who spend long stretches working at a computer. A small animated companion seemed more inviting than another timer notification, and we were curious whether users could shape a simple routine from reusable activity blocks.
submission.what_it_does: The desktop prototype lets a user set a work interval and shows a small animated character when it is time to pause. A break screen offers a few hand and wrist exercises with a timer and an encouraging message when the interval ends. We sketched a visual workflow builder for arranging break steps, but it is not connected to the timer yet.
submission.how_we_built_it: We used Python, Tkinter, and Pillow to create the timer window, exercise cards, and animated desktop pet. The timer triggers the break screen, which reads from a small list of exercises and messages; the pet reacts to the timer state. Separately, we made a mock canvas for arranging routine blocks, inspired by visual agent builders, but it does not yet generate or run a routine.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Transparent-looking desktop windows and keeping the pet in place took experimentation. We also hoped to infer activity from computer use, but platform-specific permissions and hardware differences made that too large for the weekend. The routine canvas and timer remain separate pieces.
submission.accomplishments: We got the timer, break prompt, and draggable character working together as a basic desktop flow. We are pleased that the prototype can offer a choice of exercises instead of only displaying a generic alert.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned Tkinter event handling, basic animation, and how to keep user choices in a simple desktop interface. We also learned from trying a visual workflow canvas that blocks only help when they connect to real behavior, and AI coding assistance needed review to keep the implementation small.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the routine canvas to the timer, add more break activities, and make the companion customizable. Later, we could explore cross-platform activity signals and optional hardware reminders, with clear controls over what the app observes.

challenge_results.rationale: The submission shows a working desktop garden prototype with an animated companion and exercise prompts, but the routine builder is not yet connected to the timer.

submission.name: Invoice Pantry
submission.tagline: Sort upcoming bills into a practical next step for a small finance team.
submission.inspiration: We wanted to make routine bill tracking less scattered for student organizations and small campus groups. It is easy to lose track of which expenses are due soon when invoices and reminders live in different places.
submission.what_it_does: Invoice Pantry lets a user enter bills, due dates, and a few payment preferences, then highlights what needs attention first. It can suggest a simple payment order and show the reason behind each suggestion; voice entry and the guided review flow are rough prototypes.
submission.how_we_built_it: We made a web app with a React interface and a Node backend, using MongoDB for group, bill, and preference data. A scoring flow uses due dates and entered constraints to rank bills, while a voice input experiment tries to turn spoken expenses into fields the user can confirm.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: Voice transcription and parsing were inconsistent, especially when people said amounts or dates casually. The demo does not work end-to-end: the bill list and ranking can run separately, but voice entry and saving a reviewed bill do not reliably connect.
submission.accomplishments: We got the main bill-entry screen and an explainable priority list working as separate pieces. We are proud that the ranking makes its reasoning visible instead of presenting a payment order without context.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that a useful finance tool needs dependable data entry and clear handling of missing details before adding smart suggestions. Gemini helped us explore ways to summarize why a bill was surfaced, but we still needed a person to check the extracted information.
submission.whats_next: We would connect the review flow to persistent bill records and make date and amount confirmation more reliable. Later, we would add shared access for a group treasurer and test the ranking against real payment workflows.

challenge_results.rationale: Invoice Pantry addresses a meaningful financial process improvement for small teams with a practical bill tracking system, using a React/Node stack and explainable prioritization logic, though voice input and workflow integration remain incomplete.

submission.name: Reserve Relay
submission.tagline: Turn small purchase roundups into a shared emergency reserve, with a live view of the work behind each suggestion.
submission.inspiration: We were interested in making it easier for community groups to build a modest cash buffer from everyday activity. We paired automated roundup calculations with the idea of a coordinated agent team that can explain and check a financial workflow.
submission.what_it_does: Reserve Relay reads sample transactions, calculates the difference to the next dollar, and shows how those amounts could build a reserve. A small set of AI agents handles transaction categorization, summarizes spending patterns, and flags items that need review; the app can also send a simulated transfer to a Solana Devnet wallet.
submission.how_we_built_it: A FastAPI service connects a Nessie transaction feed, roundup calculations, Gemini-generated summaries, and Solana Devnet transfers to a React dashboard. We used separate agent roles for categorization, insight writing, and review, and stream their status to the interface so users can see which step is running.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The complete demo runs with sample data, but categorization sometimes assigns a transaction to the wrong spending group, which can skew the generated advice. We also found that tiny decimal amounts need careful conversion before they become token units.
submission.accomplishments: We connected the sample transaction flow to roundup totals, an AI explanation, and a testnet transfer. The live agent activity view helped us make the otherwise hidden processing steps easier to follow.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that multiple AI roles are useful only when their handoffs and outputs are easy to inspect. Gemini helped draft plain-language summaries, while we learned to keep calculations and transfer amounts in deterministic code.
submission.whats_next: We would improve categorization review, add configurable reserve goals, and support more transaction sources. Before any real financial use, we would also need stronger security and a careful review of transfer and account requirements.

challenge_results.rationale: Reserve Relay improves a financial process by automating small purchase roundups for community reserves, with a 3/5 relevance to financial services.

submission.name: Crew Cutback
submission.tagline: Help campus volunteer crews spend less on last-minute meals and snacks.
submission.inspiration: Our volunteer teams often make food runs between events and lose track of how much those trips add up to. We wanted a friendly way for crews to set a shared limit and keep each other aware of the spending.
submission.what_it_does: A crew can set a weekly food-spending target, log purchases, and see a group total alongside a lightweight leaderboard. Members can manually log a stop or use location prompts to check whether they bought anything; Gemini can offer a short summary of the crew's recent pattern.
submission.how_we_built_it: We built a React Native app with Expo and TypeScript, backed by Firebase for crew, member, and purchase records. Location checks can prompt a member to enter a purchase, and Gemini turns the saved totals into a brief recap rather than making budgeting decisions.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: The app works through the main logging and group view, but location prompts can arrive late or fail when the app is in the background. We also had package and device setup issues that made it hard to reproduce the same behavior on every phone.
submission.accomplishments: We got crews, purchase logging, and a shared spending view connected in one mobile prototype. We are glad the manual entry option still lets the group keep a record when location detection misses a stop.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how Firebase data and a React Native interface fit together for a shared mobile app. Gemini was useful for drafting concise summaries, but the underlying purchase records needed to stay visible so members could check what the summary was based on.
submission.whats_next: We would make background location behavior more dependable and add a quick correction flow for mistaken prompts. We would also explore non-food group costs, such as supplies for recurring volunteer events.

challenge_results.rationale: The app addresses a specific financial process for student volunteer groups by tracking shared food spending with a leaderboard and summaries, but has partial working core and plausible technical connections.
